title: Deep learning-based super-resolution reconstruction for improved image quality in shoulder MRI.
abstract: Purpose To compare the image quality of shoulder Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) using three imaging acquisition or reconstruction approaches-Parallel Imaging (PI), Compressed Sensing (CS), and Deep Learning-Based Super-Resolution Reconstruction (SR)-and to evaluate reader-assessed image quality and preference. Methods A retrospective study included 60 patients (27 males, 33 females; mean age 53.67 ± 12.11 years). Shoulder MRI was performed with PI, CS and SR (reconstructed from CS data) across six sequences. Quantitative and qualitative assessments were conducted by experienced observers. Three radiologists selected clinically preferred sequences after a 2-week washout. Consistency and inter-group comparisons were statistically analyzed. Results The quantitative and qualitative assessment between observers showed good consistency. The SR group showed significantly higher quantitative measurements across all six sequences of structures [e.g. SNR: Supraspinatus tendon SR 14.03 (10.60, 20.26), CS 11.87 (8.39, 15.96), PI 8.75 (5.18, 13.51), P < 0.001] than PI and CS. SR images generally showed lower edge rise distance (ERD) values, significant overall differences among PI, CS, and SR (P < 0.01), Qualitative assessment revealed that SR overall differences among PI, CS and SR, with statistically significant differences (P < 0.001). Furthermore, three reader preference results indicated a preference for SR images that all readers preferred SR images (86 %, 92 %, and 93 %). Conclusion Compared to PI and CS, SR significantly improves image quality in shoulder MRI without increasing acquisition time. SR enhances the visualization of fine anatomical structures, providing improved image quality and supporting its potential application in clinical shoulder MRI.

title: Routine pelvic MRI-derived marrow markers for predicting lumbar QCT-defined bone status using chemical shift-encoded fat quantification and radiomics.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate whether pelvic MRI-derived IDEAL-IQ parameters and T1-weighted radiomics can predict lumbar QCT-defined bone status in cancer survivors undergoing routine pelvic oncologic MRI. Materials & methods This secondary analysis within a prospective surveillance cohort included 123 patients with pelvic malignancies who underwent MRI (with IDEAL-IQ) and lumbar QCT within three months. QCT-derived volumetric BMD at T12-L2 served as the reference standard to classify subjects as normal, osteopenia, or osteoporotic. Pelvic MRI-derived PDFF and R2* were measured at the femoral head, femoral neck, and ilium; a radiomics pipeline was built on T1-weighted images. Inter-reader reliability used absolute-agreement intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Discrimination was evaluated with one-vs-rest ROC analysis, and clinical utility was assessed by decision-curve analysis using out-of-fold probabilities from five-fold internal validation for two decisions: osteoporosis versus non-osteoporosis and low bone mass versus normal bone status. Results PDFF increased and R2* decreased with worsening BMD at all sites (P < 0.05), with good inter-reader agreement (single-measurement ICCs, 0.756-0.988; mean-of-three-reader ICCs, 0.903-0.996). In internal validation, T1-weighted radiomics and IDEAL-IQ demonstrated comparable discrimination for three-class bone status (AUC 0.73-0.78). Class-wise analysis showed near-chance discrimination for osteopenia, indicating that the overall macro-AUC was mainly driven by normal-versus-osteoporosis separation. Models incorporating MRI-derived markers showed higher validation macro-AUCs than the simplified age-and-sex clinical baseline. Decision-curve analysis showed positive net benefit for both imaging-based approaches, but between-modality differences were small and should be interpreted cautiously because confidence intervals overlapped. Conclusion Pelvic MRI-derived IDEAL-IQ and radiomics markers showed modest and comparable performance for predicting lumbar QCT-defined bone status. Their discrimination was mainly driven by separation between normal bone status and osteoporosis, whereas osteopenia remained poorly distinguished. These findings support exploratory opportunistic risk flagging rather than complete three-class risk stratification.

title: DuDoTransGAN: Dual-Domain transformer based generative adversarial unsupervised network for metal artifact reduction in paired and unpaired CT.
abstract: Purpose Metal artifacts from implants degrade CT image quality, while supervised metal artifact reduction (MAR) methods require paired clean data that are rarely available clinically. Methods In this retrospective study, we developed DuDoTransGAN, an unsupervised dual-domain generative adversarial network for paired and unpaired training. It was evaluated on a publicly available paired synthetic dataset (SYN; 90,000 training and 2,000 test slices) and a clinical unpaired knee CT dataset (KNE; 19,032 slices from 66 patients; mean age, 55.8 ± 16.1 years; 36 males), including 6,168 slices with metal artifacts. On KNE, two radiologists independently assessed five image-quality aspects using Likert scales, with ratings reviewed by a senior radiologist. Results In the paired SYN experiment, DuDoTransGAN achieved a mean PSNR of 38.19 dB, the highest mean SSIM (0.975), and the lowest mean RMSE (5.65) among unsupervised methods. Performance remained stable with increasing metal-mask size, demonstrating robustness under larger-metal-mask conditions. In the unpaired KNE experiment, inter-rater agreement was excellent (ICC, 0.941). DuDoTransGAN achieved the highest mean scores among unsupervised methods for artifact removal (3.87 ± 0.48), diagnostic value (3.75 ± 0.50), visual effect (3.90 ± 0.36), and detail retention (3.96 ± 0.40), together with a comparable sharpness score (3.87 ± 0.58), and the highest radiologist selection rate (45 % vs 2 %-21 %). Conclusion DuDoTransGAN is an adaptable unsupervised dual-domain MAR framework that performs effectively on paired synthetic and unpaired clinical data, producing high-quality, clinically interpretable CT images in the presence of metallic implants.

title: Automated segmentation-based emergency CT radiomics for predicting functional outcome at discharge and in-hospital post-stroke pneumonia in primary brainstem hemorrhage.
abstract: Background Primary brainstem hemorrhage (PBSH) is associated with high mortality, disability, and uncertain early outcomes. Emergency non-contrast CT (NCCT) is the earliest imaging examination, but conventional assessment may not fully capture hematoma heterogeneity. This study aimed to develop an automated segmentation-based emergency NCCT radiomics framework for predicting poor functional outcome at discharge and in-hospital post-stroke pneumonia (PSP) in PBSH. Methods This retrospective study included 372 patients with PBSH, comprising a training set (n = 182), an internal test set (n = 79), and a temporal internal validation set (n = 111). Hematomas were segmented using a three-dimensional U-Net. Manual and automated segmentation-based radiomics models were compared, and automated segmentation-derived radiomics features were integrated with conventional radiological predictors to construct combined models for poor functional outcome and PSP. Results The automated segmentation-based radiomics model showed comparable performance to the manual segmentation-based model across all three datasets. The combined prognostic model achieved AUCs of 0.926, 0.923, and 0.858 in the training, internal test, and temporal internal validation sets, with higher AUCs and lower Brier scores than the conventional radiological model. The combined PSP model (AUCs: 0.828, 0.742, 0.681) showed no consistent improvement. SHAP identified hematoma classification as the most influential prognostic predictor. Conclusions Automated segmentation-based NCCT radiomics is feasible for early risk stratification in PBSH. The combined prognostic model showed good discrimination and potential complementary value beyond conventional CT assessment. The PSP model remains exploratory and requires further refinement and validation.

title: MRI-derived radiomics for prostate cancer active surveillance: a systematic review.
abstract: Purpose To systematically review MRI-derived radiomic and artificial intelligence models predicting outcomes in men on or eligible for active surveillance (AS) for prostate cancer, and whether reported endpoints permit quantitative synthesis. Method Following PRISMA 2020, we searched PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science (2000-September 2026). Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias (QUADAS-2, PROBAST) and methodological quality (METRICS). Three subgroups were defined: AS selection at diagnosis, baseline detection of clinically significant cancer, and progression during follow-up. Pooling was pre-specified for subgroups with at least four independent cohorts; endpoint equivalence was assessed. Results Seventeen studies across 12 unique cohorts were included. Seven publications derived from two cohorts; 12 independent cohort-level estimates (n = 2703) remained after overlap resolution. Nine publications (four independent cohorts) addressed progression (AUC 0.70 to 0.95), but progression was defined in five non-equivalent ways, from any grade-group increase to composite core-count criteria, precluding quantitative synthesis. Risk of bias was high or unclear in 16 of 17 studies; the median METRICS score was 32.3 % (range 18.9-52.3 %). No study reported external validation or calibration for progression. Conclusions Progression endpoints were heterogeneous and several were of limited clinical relevance. A core outcome set for AS (at least ISUP grade group ≥3 and/or unequivocal radiological progression), followed by multi-centre external validation with a head-to-head comparison against the PRECISE v2 (Prostate Cancer Radiological Estimation of Change in Sequential Evaluation) score, is the priority before clinical use can be considered.

Seventeen studies across 12 unique cohorts were included. Seven publications derived from two cohorts; 12 independent cohort-level estimates (n = 2703) remained after overlap resolution. Nine publications (four independent cohorts) addressed progression (AUC 0.70 to 0.95), but progression was defined in five non-equivalent ways, from any grade-group increase to composite core-count criteria, precluding quantitative synthesis. Risk of bias was high or unclear in 16 of 17 studies; the median METRICS score was 32.3 % (range 18.9-52.3 %). No study reported external validation or calibration for progression.

Conclusions

Progression endpoints were heterogeneous and several were of limited clinical relevance. A core outcome set for AS (at least ISUP grade group ≥3 and/or unequivocal radiological progression), followed by multi-centre external validation with a head-to-head comparison against the PRECISE v2 (Prostate Cancer Radiological Estimation of Change in Sequential Evaluation) score, is the priority before clinical use can be considered.

title: Medical image analysis for three-dimensional reconstruction in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: Imaging inputs, reconstruction methods, validation evidence, and research gaps.
abstract: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a complex three-dimensional (3D) spinal deformity. Although standing full-spine radiography remains the cornerstone of clinical diagnosis and longitudinal follow-up, two-dimensional projections cannot fully characterize vertebral rotation, local osseous geometry, or global spatial alignment. In recent years, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), conventional radiography, EOS/biplanar radiography, 3D ultrasound, and surface imaging have increasingly been integrated with deep learning, statistical shape modeling, and generative approaches, substantially expanding the technical pathways for patient-specific 3D reconstruction in AIS. However, substantial heterogeneity remains across studies with respect to input constraints, target populations, reference standards, and validation endpoints, and the evidentiary boundaries between technical performance, AIS-specific validity, and clinical validity have not been systematically clarified. This review adopted a structured methodological framework and systematically searched the Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed/MEDLINE, and IEEE Xplore, supplemented by forward and backward citation tracking. Study-level evidence was synthesized across imaging inputs, reconstruction tasks, algorithmic paradigms, and validation designs. A total of 115 core studies were included, comprising 32 AIS-specific studies (27.8%), 21 scoliosis-specific or mixed-population studies (18.3%), and 62 studies based on general spinal-image-analysis evidence (53.9%). Based on the reference standards and validation endpoints used, we established a five-level validation framework ranging from image/segmentation-level validation (L1), anatomical-structure-level validation (L2), and clinical-parameter-level validation (L3), to workflow/generalization-level validation (L4) and clinical-translation-level validation (L5). An evidence-gap matrix based on "imaging modality × methodological task" was also constructed. Among the 115 studies, 28 (24.3%) reached a maximum of L1, 49 (42.6%) reached L2, 34 (29.6%) reached L3, and only 4 (3.5%) reached L4; no study met the L5 criteria, and no explicit AIS-specific external validation was identified. Current evidence indicates that CT provides a strong basis for high-fidelity osseous reconstruction, EOS has accumulated relatively continuous AIS-specific evidence for weight-bearing 3D parameter assessment, and 3D ultrasound offers advantages for repeated radiation-free parameter measurement, whereas MRI-based reconstruction and limited-projection 3D recovery remain rapidly evolving fields. The principal challenge has therefore shifted from whether a 3D structure can be generated to whether structural fidelity can be translated into reliable clinical parameters and whether models can generalize consistently across independent AIS populations, imaging systems, and acquisition protocols. Future work should prioritize AIS-specific multicenter validation resources, task-matched 3D reference standards, and a continuous evidence chain linking structural fidelity, clinical-parameter validity, external generalization, and clinical impact, thereby advancing AIS 3D reconstruction from technical feasibility toward trustworthy clinical application.

title: Periprostatic adipose tissue imaging in prostate cancer: Imaging phenotypes, task-specific spatial strategies, and multicompartment integration-a critical review.
abstract: Purpose To appraise how periprostatic adipose tissue (PPAT) is defined, sampled, and evaluated in prostate cancer imaging, with emphasis on spatial strategy, intended clinical use, evidence maturity, and imaging-tissue correspondence. Method We conducted a structured critical review with evidence mapping, supported by PubMed/MEDLINE and Web of Science searches through August 29, 2026, supplemented by prespecified Google Scholar and citation searches. Two reviewers independently screened records. Reports were mapped by imaging strategy, spatial target, clinical task, evaluation design, reproducibility, cohort overlap, and imaging-tissue correspondence. Results The formal evidence set comprised 113 reports, including 63 clinical imaging reports. Strategies comprised morphometry / computed tomography (CT) attenuation (48 reports), tissue-property / compositional imaging (4), PPAT-focused radiomics (4), and interface / multicompartment modelling (7). Quantitative reproducibility was reported in 19/63 clinical reports. Only two reports underwent independent external evaluation, and neither evaluated a PPAT-only model. Biological and translational evidence supported PPAT as a heterogeneous tumour-adjacent compartment, whereas direct spatially matched imaging-tissue validation remained uncommon. Clinical evidence spanned prebiopsy risk refinement, upgrading or active-surveillance reclassification, local extension and surgical planning, prognosis, treatment-related outcomes, and nodal and metastatic assessment; most reports lacked independent evaluation. Conclusions PPAT imaging is best regarded as a set of spatially defined, task-specific phenotypes rather than a single biomarker. Current evidence positions PPAT as a candidate adjunct to established clinical and intraprostatic imaging information. Clinical adoption will require reproducible definitions and measurements, task-matched assessment of incremental value, independent external evaluation, and prospective evidence of decision impact.

title: Photon-counting CT based vestibular aqueduct trajectory analysis for the assessment of Ménière's disease endotypes and hearing loss.
abstract: Background Ménière's disease (MD) is a heterogeneous inner ear disorder, and imaging-based endotype identification may inform prognosis and personalized management. The vestibular aqueduct (VA) is a candidate imaging biomarker, and photon-counting CT (PCCT) offers high-resolution depiction of temporal bone microanatomy. This study evaluated PCCT-derived VA morphometric parameters as imaging biomarkers for MD endotype identification and hearing loss assessment. Methods In this retrospective study, 106 patients (212 ears) underwent temporal bone PCCT and 3.0-T 3D-FLAIR MRI. PCCT parameters included angular trajectory of the VA (ATVA), VA visibility grade, morphologic subtype, midpoint width, VA length, and posterior semicircular canal-posterior fossa distance. Two neuroradiologists independently evaluated all images. Diagnostic performance for six clinically motivated tasks was assessed by AUC with leave-one-patient-out cross-validation (LOPOCV); associations with pure-tone average (PTA) were evaluated by multivariable linear regression with cluster-robust standard errors. Results Interobserver agreement was excellent (ICC, 0.84-0.91). VA visibility grading identified the hypoplastic endotype with an AUC of 0.860 (LOPOCV, 0.812); combined VA morphology and midpoint width distinguished the degenerated endotype with an AUC of 0.784 (LOPOCV, 0.736). Multivariable regression identified ATVA as an independent PTA predictor (β = 0.238, p = 0.023). Conclusions PCCT-derived VA morphometric parameters enabled MD endotype identification despite clinical heterogeneity and were associated with hearing loss severity, supporting their potential role as imaging biomarkers for MD management.

title: Opportunistic screening of hip osteoporosis using Phantom-Less quantitative CT-Derived thoracic volumetric BMD from routine chest CT: A Multicentre, retrospective study.
abstract: Objective To develop and validate diagnostic thresholds for thoracic volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD) derived from routine chest CT scans, and to evaluate the performance of this metric for opportunistic screening of hip osteoporosis (hOP) and hip osteopenia in adults aged 60 years and older. Methods This multicenter retrospective study enrolled 568 patients aged 60 years and older who underwent both non-contrast chest computed tomography (CT) and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA). Thoracic quantitative CT-derived volumetric bone mineral density (Th-vBMD) was measured using a phantomless quantitative CT (PL-QCT) system. The robustness of the diagnostic model was evaluated through internal validation, including 500-iteration bootstrap resampling. The diagnostic performance of Th-vBMD was compared against the reference hip DXA T-score. Results A total of 568 patients were included. The prevalence of hOP and hip osteopenia was 36.3 % and 42.6 %, respectively. Th-vBMD demonstrated performance with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.873 (95 % CI: 0.837-0.910). The optimal Th-vBMD threshold for hOP was 85.4 mg/cm 3 , sensitivity 0.851 and specificity 0.864. The optimal threshold for hip osteopenia was 120.7 mg/cm 3 , sensitivity: 0.860 and specificity: 0.811. Logistic regression identified Th-vBMD ≤ 85.4 mg/cm 3 as an independent predictor of hOP (adjusted OR: 26.70; 95 % CI: 16.3-45.0; p < 0.001). Conclusion This study establishes and validates Th-vBMD thresholds derived from routine chest CT for opportunistic hOP screening in elderly. This cost-effective strategy leverages clinical imaging data to identify individuals at osteoporosis risk, facilitating intervention and advancing osteoporosis prevention.

title: Region-specific associations between dual-Layer spectral detector CT-derived carotid plaque parameters and white matter hyperintensity burden in patients with carotid atherosclerosis.
abstract: Objective White matter hyperintensities (WMH) exhibit region-specific characteristics. Whether dual-layer spectral detector CT (DLSCT)-derived plaque parameters associate with WMH burden region-specifically remains unclear. Methods This cross-sectional study enrolled 213 patients with carotid atherosclerotic plaques who underwent carotid CTA and brain MRI within 30 days. Seven DLSCT parameters were measured; WMH was segmented into juxtaventricular, periventricular, deep, and juxtacortical subregions. Multivariable linear regression assessed associations with total WMH burden (FDR correction). Nested models evaluated incremental value. Linear mixed-effects models with region-by-parameter interactions assessed region-specific associations. Results In the primary model (Model 2), Z-Zeff was significantly negatively associated with total WMH burden (β = -0.205, 95 % CI: -0.299 ∼ -0.111, FDR-q < 0.001). Adding Z-Zeff to the clinical model significantly increased explained variance (ΔR 2 = 0.070, p < 0.001, ΔAIC = -15.09), whereas conventional CTA parameters did not (ΔR 2 = 0.001, p = 0.938). Significant region interactions were observed for Z-Zeff, age, and LDL-C. Z-Zeff was negatively associated with all subregions, strongest in periventricular (β = -0.254) and deep (β = -0.172) WMH. Age was most strongly associated with periventricular WMH (β = 0.436). LDL-C and diabetes were associated only with periventricular WMH (β = -0.111 and -0.221, respectively). Conclusion DLSCT-derived Z-Zeff was independently associated with WMH burden in a region-specific manner, with the strongest associations in periventricular and deep white matter, and provided incremental value beyond clinical and conventional CTA parameters. These findings support Z-Zeff as a potential imaging biomarker linking carotid plaque composition to regional cerebral small vessel disease.

title: Incorporating visceral adipose tissue into dual-region deep learning radiomics on CT improves preoperative lymph node metastasis prediction in gastric cancer: A multicenter study.
abstract: Background Visceral adipose tissue (VAT) is associated with tumor progression in gastric cancer (GC), but its added value for predicting lymph node metastasis (LNM) remains unclear. Purpose This study aimed to construct a DR-DLR model that incorporates CT-based features from both VAT and tumor, with the goal of predicting LNM in GC patients, while investigating its biological relevance. Methods 855 GC patients were retrospectively collected across three clinical centers, divided into a primary cohort, one internal test cohort, and two independent external validation cohorts. An Attention Residual Transformation Network (ARTNet) extracted imaging representations from CT images. Feature representations and clinical variables were integrated using a multilayer perceptron (MLP) to build the DR-DLR model. Model performance, generalizability, prognostic value, and biological relevance were evaluated using internal/external testing, radiologist comparison, survival analysis, and radiogenomics analysis. Results Incorporation of VAT-derived features improved predictive performance compared with tumor-only models. The DR-DLR model achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.898 (95 % CI: 0.817-0.946), 0.834 (95 % CI: 0.743-0.897), and 0.848 (95 % CI: 0.775-0.901) in the internal and two external test cohorts, respectively. It outperformed junior and senior radiologists in LNM assessment. Overall survival was shorter in high-risk patients than in low-risk. Radiogenomics analysis revealed that the high-risk phenotype was associated with activation of immune-related pathways and increased infiltration of CD4 + T cells, plasma cells, dendritic cells, and mast cells. Conclusion The DR-DLR model improved LNM prediction, with its high-risk phenotype linked to immune-related molecular alterations, supporting its value for preoperative risk stratification.

title: CT-based multimodal fusion model for preoperative clear cell renal cell carcinoma grading: A multicenter study.
abstract: Objectives To develop and evaluate a multimodal fusion framework for the preoperative World Health Organization/International Society of Urological Pathology (WHO/ISUP) low- and high-grade classification of clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), integrating clinical characteristics, deep learning (DL), and radiomic signatures extracted from corticomedullary phase (CMP) contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) images. Materials and methods In this retrospective multicenter study, we evaluated a cohort of 1,052 patients with histologically verified ccRCC across four institutions. The data of the primary cohort (Center A, n = 665) were randomly divided into a training dataset (n = 465) and an internal validation dataset (n = 200). The data of 387 additional patients from three institutions (Centers B-D) constituted the independent external test set. Initial single-modality classifiers were developed via ensemble machine learning, utilizing clinical variables, multiscale radiomic data (capturing intratumoral, habitat, and peritumoral regions), and DL representations (2D, 2.5D, and 3D). A soft voting mechanism was subsequently applied to integrate the top-performing base models. Model interpretability was determined using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values, and overall diagnostic efficacy was quantified through receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Results The weighted soft voting model (SoftVote-Opt) showed the numerically highest AUC among the evaluated fusion strategies and single-modality models. This model yielded AUCs of 0.761 (95 % CI: 0.675-0.839) and 0.745 (95 % CI: 0.675-0.813), with corresponding MCCs of 0.347 (95 % CI: 0.217-0.475) and 0.302(95 % CI: 0.205 -0.387), within the internal validation and external test sets, respectively. SHAP analysis revealed peritumoral 5 mm radiomic features as the primary determinants of the model's output, followed by intratumoral radiomic features, whereas deep learning and clinical features offered lower relative contributions. Conclusion The multimodal fusion framework demonstrated moderate discriminatory performance across the internal validation and external test cohorts. These findings could be regarded as an exploratory study rather than evidence of established clinical superiority. The framework may provide complementary information for preoperative ccRCC grading. Critical relevance statement This study evaluates an exploratory multimodal fusion framework for preoperative ccRCC grading by combining clinical data, deep learning, and multiscale radiomic features. The framework may provide complementary non-invasive information for risk stratification.

title: Toward truly agentic radiology AI: A multimodal architecture framework and differentiated implementation roadmap.
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence(AI) represents a structural transition from task-specific tools to autonomous systems capable of goal-oriented, multi-step reasoning. However, translating this potential into radiology requires a fundamental shift from text-dominated architectures to avision-first approachthat engages the specialty's diagnostic core. In this paper, we characterize the multimodal challenge distinguishing radiology from text-centric domains, where high-dimensional images serve as the primary diagnostic substrate rather than supplementary data. We reviewthree image-text coupling architectures, their clinical capabilities, limitations, and deployment feasibility. These include output-level coupling through sequential image-text pipelines, representation-level coupling through contrastive aligned dual encoders, and token-level coupling through generative vision-language models. To guide development, we introduce afive-level taxonomy of autonomy(Levels 1-5), establishing clear validation checkpoints and regulatory expectations for increasing machine independence, from text-based workflow automation to fully autonomous closed-loop systems. We emphasize that interoperability via standardized protocols, includingDICOMweb, HL7-FHIR, Model Context Protocol (MCP), and Agent2Agent (A2A), is as critical as the AI models themselves. Finally, we address critical implementation guardrails, including mitigatingalgorithmic hallucinations, defending againstadversarial prompt injection, and preserving human diagnostic proficiency amidst the risk of AI-induced skill decay. This comprehensive roadmap provides a structured path for integrating autonomous visual reasoning into modern medical imaging environments.

title: Ultra-high-resolution 5 T MR neurography: first steps.
abstract: Magnetic resonance neurography (MRN) is an established technique for peripheral nerve assessment, enabling high-resolution visualization of nerves and simultaneous evaluation of adjacent musculoskeletal structures. Although optimized 3 T MRI remains the clinical standard, whole-body 5 T systems have emerged as a potential intermediate platform between 3 T and 7 T imaging. Direct peer-reviewed evidence for peripheral MRN at 5 T remains limited to a single pilot study of the inferior alveolar nerve, with no prospective validation of the brachial plexus, lumbosacral plexus, or limb nerves. Physical and engineering studies suggest that 5 T MRI may provide greater signal availability than 3 T while presenting less severe radiofrequency-related challenges than 7 T; however, the relevance of this theoretical balance to peripheral nerve imaging remains unproven. The additional signal available at 5 T could theoretically be allocated to higher spatial resolution, greater acceleration, or broader anatomical coverage, but these potential gains have not been validated against optimized 3 T MRN. Potential applications include the evaluation of entrapment neuropathies, traumatic nerve injuries, inflammatory neuropathies, peripheral nerve tumors, and the implementation of quantitative approaches such as diffusion tensor imaging, T2 mapping, and T1ρ imaging. Furthermore, artificial intelligence-based reconstruction, denoising, and acceleration strategies may improve the clinical feasibility of ultra-high-resolution neurography by reducing scan times while preserving image quality. This narrative review examines the limited published evidence, physical rationale, technical requirements, preliminary institutional experience, and research priorities for 5 T MRN.

title: Pancreatic mucinous cystic neoplasms in adults: An update on the role of CT and MRI for risk stratification.
abstract: Pancreatic mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCNs) are characterized histologically by an inner mucin-producing columnar epithelium supported by a dense ovarian-type stroma. MCNs account for approximately 10% of pancreatic cystic neoplasms. Surgical resection is the treatment of choice, as MCNs may harbor high-grade dysplasia or progress to invasive carcinoma. Establishing reliable imaging criteria for risk stratification is critical to identify patients who are candidates for surgery. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging play pivotal roles in lesion characterization and assessment of features associated with high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma. Current guidelines recognize several imaging features as high-risk characteristics for MCNs, including large tumor size, mural nodules, and main pancreatic duct dilatation. However, other potential predictors of malignancy remain poorly defined and are not sufficiently emphasized. The strongest MCN-specific evidence, as demonstrated in multivariable analyses, supports larger cyst size, mural nodules, main pancreatic duct dilatation, and, in selected cohorts, elevated serum cancer antigen 19-9. Male sex has also been associated with malignancy in retrospective surgical cohorts, whereas pancreatic head/neck location, calcification, wall/septal thickening, age, and signal heterogeneity on T2-weighted images remain less consistently validated. Importantly, most malignancy-prediction literature is based on resected, pathologically confirmed MCNs and is therefore vulnerable to selection and verification bias and cannot be directly extrapolated to all incidentally detected presumed MCNs. This article presents a transparent literature search methodology and an evidence-based synthesis of predictors of malignancy that clearly distinguishes MCN-specific multivariable evidence from lower-level or extrapolated data. It also provides a comparison of key guidelines. Unlike previous reviews, this article directly addresses the evidence gap between resection-based cohorts and the broader population of incidentally detected presumed MCNs. It also clarifies when imaging findings should prompt further evaluation rather than independently determine management.

title: Background parenchymal enhancement in ultrafast MRI: Inter-reader agreement before and after training, and correlations with prognostic factors of breast cancer.
abstract: Purpose To assess the inter-reader agreement in background parenchymal enhancement (BPE) categorization on ultrafast dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) MRI before and after training and its relationship with breast cancer prognostic factors. Materials and methods We retrospectively analyzed the cases of 220 patients (median, age 60 years; 220 breast cancers) who underwent ultrafast DCE MRI. BPE was qualitatively classified as minimal, mild, moderate, or marked by three readers: Reader1 (R1), a radiology resident in the second year of training; Reader2 (R2), an experienced general radiologist with 28 years of experience in diagnostic radiology; and Reader3 (R3), an experienced breast radiologist with 25 years of experience in breast MRI. Inter-reader agreement was evaluated using weighted kappa (κ) values and was reassessed between R1 and R3 after intensive training. Associations between BPE levels and prognostic factors were also evaluated. Results Inter-reader agreement was substantial with weighted κ values of 0.679-0.742 for R1 versus R2, 0.612-0.665 for R1 versus R3, and 0.626-0.689 for R2 versus R3. Agreement between R1 and R3 improved slightly after training but remained substantial. No significant associations were observed between visual BPE classification and prognostic factors, including hormone receptor status, HER2 status, and proliferation markers. Conclusion Inter-reader agreement for BPE assessment on ultrafast DCE MRI was substantial and improved slightly after training. No significant relationship was observed between ultrafast BPE and breast cancer prognostic factors.

title: An integrated pathological-radiological downstaging score for prognostic classification in gastric cancer after neoadjuvant chemotherapy: A multicenter retrospective study.
abstract: Background Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) followed by surgery is the standard treatment for locally advanced gastric cancer (LAGC). However, post-therapy staging based on ypTNM mainly reflects residual pathological status and does not capture pretreatment disease burden or the extent of tumor regression after NAC, limiting postoperative prognostic stratification. To address this limitation, we developed a Pathological-Radiological Integrated Model (PRIM) that combines baseline stage, post-treatment pathology, and radiologic response. Methods We enrolled 414 patients with LAGC who underwent radical gastrectomy after NAC, including 348 in a development cohort and 66 in an external validation cohort. A Down-stage System (DS) was constructed to quantify tumor stage changes after NAC by weighting cT/cN and ypT/ypN categories using multivariable Cox regression. title: CT semantic features versus first-order histogram analysis for preoperative prediction of Lauren classification in gastric cancer.
abstract: Objectives Accurate preoperative prediction of gastric cancer Lauren subtypes is critical for individualized treatment decision-making. This study aimed to explore and compare CT-based semantic features, first-order histogram analysis, and their combined model for non-invasive discrimination of intestinal and diffuse Lauren subtypes of gastric cancer. Methods This retrospective study enrolled 140 patients with gastric cancer, who were randomly assigned to a training set (n = 98) and an internal validation set (n = 42). The collected variables included clinical data, conventional CT indicators (e.g., peritoneal metastasis, tumor size, and thickness), and first-order histogram features extracted from the primary tumor and peritoneum (e.g., mean, entropy, skewness). The endpoint was Lauren classification (intestinal vs. diffuse type). Three predictive models, including a CT semantic model, a first-order histogram radiomic model, and a combined model, were established using LASSO logistic regression. Model performance was comprehensively evaluated in terms of discriminative ability, calibration, and clinical net benefit. Results All three models achieved robust discriminative performance. The first-order radiomic model yielded the highest training-set AUC (0.904), followed by the combined model (0.879) and CT semantic model (0.844). Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons showed no significant inter-model differences, demonstrating comparable predictive efficacy. Owing to its non-inferior performance and superior clinical accessibility, the CT semantic model was visualized as a nomogram for individualized preoperative Lauren subtype assessment. While calibration was satisfactory in the training cohort, mild calibration drift with a reduced slope and increased maximum calibration error was observed in internal validation, though discriminative power remained acceptable. DCA confirmed favourable clinical net benefit across a wide range of risk thresholds in both training and validation cohorts. Conclusions Both the CT semantic features model and the first-order histogram model enable reliable preoperative Lauren subtype prediction. Featuring higher accessibility, the CT semantic features model needs no extra radiomic analysis. Though exploratory, these non-invasive tools may enable preoperative subtype identification and individualized treatment planning.

title: Core Descriptor Set for Studies Evaluating Interventions for Chronic Deep Venous Diseases.
abstract: Objective Chronic deep venous disease (CDVD) is a common and debilitating disease resulting in significant morbidity and costs. However, inconsistent reporting of patient characteristics in CDVD hinders study comparability and limits opportunities for data synthesis. This study aimed to develop a core descriptor set (CDS) for studies evaluating interventions for CDVD of the lower limbs. Methods Candidate descriptors were identified from published literature and stakeholder recommendations. Vascular surgeons, haematologists, interventional radiologists, and nurse specialists took part in two rounds of an international modified Delphi process using a nine point Likert scale to rank descriptor importance. Descriptors not meeting consensus criteria in the first round were re-evaluated in round two. Descriptors meeting the criteria for critical importance were discussed in a final meeting between international specialists to finalise the CDS. Results One hundred and thirty-eight Delphi participants were recruited from 29 countries. Ninety-eight descriptors were longlisted from the literature, refined to 84 by the steering group. After round one, 23 descriptors achieved consensus and were removed from subsequent rounds. Seven newly proposed descriptors were then added, resulting in a total of 68 descriptors in round two. Following round two, a further 13 descriptors achieved consensus with eight considered borderline. Following two Delphi survey rounds and a consensus meeting, 84 candidate descriptors were systematically evaluated and narrowed down to a final set of 21 core descriptors across the domains of demographics, thrombotic risk, venous history, anatomy, symptoms, and clinical findings. Conclusion This study defined the CDS for CDVD, facilitating more consistent, robust, and meaningful reporting across studies and enabling reliable synthesis.

title: Venous Hypertension Associated with an Abnormal Configuration of a Protruding Cephalic Arch Stent in Arteriovenous Haemodialysis Access: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Cephalic arch stenosis is a common cause of access dysfunction in brachiocephalic arteriovenous fistulae, and recurrent lesions are often treated with stent placement. Although stent protrusion into the axillary vein is frequently tolerated, an abnormal stent-vein configuration combined with in stent re-stenosis may impair physiological venous drainage. This case report presents severe venous hypertension resulting from in stent re-stenosis within the protruding segment impairing physiological axillary venous outflow and an abnormal stent-vein configuration caused by stent tip contact with the opposite axillary vein wall, redistributing access flow. Report A 75 year old man receiving long term haemodialysis developed upper extremity oedema and prolonged post-dialysis bleeding from his brachiocephalic arteriovenous fistula. Computed tomography showed a cephalic arch stent protruding across the cephalic axillary junction, its tip contacting the axillary vein wall opposite the junction. Access fistulography demonstrated severe in stent re-stenosis with neointimal hyperplasia reducing the available sidewall openings. Through the remaining patent openings, part of the access flow continued centrally and part was redirected into the axillary venous segment peripheral to the cephalic axillary junction, with retrograde opacification and subsequent collateral drainage. The protruding stent segment was excised, and the axillary vein reconstructed with a patch. After surgery, oedema improved, collateral venous flow decreased, and the access remained functional at one year despite residual re-stenosis. Discussion This case demonstrates that cephalic arch stent protrusion may become clinically significant when in stent re-stenosis within the protruding segment impairs axillary venous outflow and the stent-vein configuration causes access flow redistribution. In this patient, neointimal hyperplasia reduced the sidewall openings, impairing physiological axillary venous outflow, while residual openings allowed redistribution of access flow into the peripheral axillary venous segment. Recognition of this abnormal stent-vein configuration and flow pattern is important because open surgical reconstruction may be required to restore venous drainage while preserving haemodialysis access function.

title: Nursing management of postoperative hemorrhagic shock: A case study in intensive care.
abstract: Introduction Postoperative hemorrhagic shock is a time-critical complication associated with high morbidity and mortality, particularly in older surgical patients, requiring rapid, coordinated management in the intensive care unit (ICU). This case report describes specialized nursing management guided by the International Classification for Nursing Practice (ICNP®/CIPE®) and Benner's Clinical Wisdom Theory. Case presentation An 89-year-old woman underwent emergency gastrojejunostomy for intestinal obstruction and subsequently developed hemorrhagic shock with profound anemia (hemoglobin nadir 5.8 g/dL), severe hyperlactatemia (12 mmol/L), hypothermia (33.6 °C), peripheral hypoperfusion, and hypotension (mean arterial pressure <65 mmHg). She required orotracheal intubation, invasive mechanical ventilation, and deep sedation. Diagnostic reassessment included serial hemoglobin and arterial blood gas analyses, lactate trending, invasive hemodynamic monitoring, and surgical re-exploration with intraoperative upper endoscopy, which suggested an upper gastrointestinal source (suspected Mallory-Weiss type lesion) treated endoscopically. Nursing priorities, structured using ICNP®, focused on perfusion restoration and correction of the lethal triad (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy), multimodal analgesia, continuous monitoring, prevention bundles (infection and pressure injury prevention), and structured family communication. Discussion The patient progressively stabilized, with hemoglobin increasing to 9.6 g/dL, lactate decreasing to <1 mmol/L, normothermia recovery, discontinuation of vasopressors, and no documented ICU-acquired complications during the ICU stay. This case highlights how standardized nursing language (ICNP®/CIPE®), combined with advanced clinical reasoning and evidence-based ICU bundles, can improve the structure, traceability, and continuity of nursing care in postoperative hemorrhagic shock.

title: Deep-learning histopathradiomics enables high-throughput quantification of pollutant-induced tissue injury in marine mussels.
abstract: Quantitative tissue-level biomarkers are important for assessing pollutant-induced biological effects, yet conventional histopathology remains largely manual, low-throughput, and observer-dependent. We developed a deep learning-based histopathradiomics workflow for high-throughput morphometric quantification in the marine mussel Mytilus galloprovincialis. Benzo[a]pyrene (BaP) was used as a benchmark stressor to provide a biologically defined tissue-injury context for workflow evaluation. An optimized Res-UNet achieved Dice coefficients of 0.9159 ± 0.0788 for gill epithelium and 0.8687 ± 0.1612 for digestive tubule walls, enabling automated quantification of 1264 gill filaments and 1437 digestive tubules within minutes. The resulting gill epithelial area and digestive tubule wall area showed injury-related patterns consistent with semi-quantitative pathology and manual thickness-based morphometry. The current binary framework focuses on predefined structural endpoints rather than the full spectrum of histopathological lesions. Without further model optimization, application to an independent sulfamethoxazole (SMX) + BaP dataset retained comparable tissue-injury patterns across exposure scenarios and independent experimental and histological batches, supporting cross-scenario applicability. Overall, this workflow transforms established histopathological biomarkers into scalable and biologically interpretable morphometric endpoints, while reducing repeated manual delineation and providing a practical basis for standardized tissue-level effect assessment in marine sentinel organisms.

title: Contralateral piriform cortex alterations after surgery for temporal lobe epilepsy: A pilot MRI volumetry study.
abstract: Purpose Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is increasingly conceptualized as a network disorder, with the piriform cortex as an implicated region. We characterized postoperative contralateral piriform cortex-cortical amygdala (PCA) structural and perfusion-related changes in a small seizure-free TLE cohort. Methods Nine patients with drug-resistant TLE who underwent epilepsy surgery and achieved postoperative seizure freedom were included in this single-center pre-post pilot study. Bilateral PCA was manually delineated on 3D T1-weighted MRI using ITK-SNAP, and volumes were normalized to total intracranial volume derived from CAT12 segmentation. Eight atlas-derived contralateral temporal lobe regions were examined as exploratory regional-specificity comparisons. In patients with available pulsed arterial spin labeling (PASL), piriform and putaminal signal intensities were measured by region-of-interest analysis. Non-parametric paired tests were used; secondary and exploratory analyses were corrected using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure. Results Normalized to total intracranial volume (TIV) contralateral PCA volume decreased postoperatively (Wilcoxon Z = -2.073, exact two-tailed p = 0.039; r = 0.69). None of the eight atlas-derived contralateral temporal regions showed a significant pre-post volume change. Contralateral putamen-normalized piriform signal intensity did not change significantly (Z = -0.105, p = 0.917), and no secondary or exploratory analysis remained significant after FDR correction. Conclusions In this hypothesis-generating pilot cohort, contralateral PCA volume decreased after epilepsy surgery, whereas the PASL-derived signal-intensity measure did not show a corresponding group-level change. These observations do not establish a surgery-induced network mechanism and require confirmation in larger controlled longitudinal cohorts.

title: Using Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance to Improve Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease Risk Stratification in Individuals with Type 2 Diabetes from Primary Care and Endocrinology Settings.
abstract: Objectives Current metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) guidelines recommend fibrosis screening in individuals with type 2 diabetes (T2D) because of their increased risk of clinically significant fibrosis (≥F2). However, fibrosis risk is variable, and clinical tools to identify individuals at lower risk are lacking. We evaluated whether assessment of insulin resistance by homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) could improve risk stratification for clinically significant fibrosis. Methods We prospectively recruited 501 adults with T2D from primary care and endocrinology clinics. Participants were classified as insulin-resistant (HOMA-IR ≥2.5; n=350) or insulin-sensitive (HOMA-IR <2.5; n=151). Liver steatosis was assessed using VCTE, MRI/MRE, or liver biopsy according to the most accurate test, and the prevalence of clinically significant fibrosis (≥F2) was compared between groups. Results Insulin-resistant participants had higher prevalence of clinically significant fibrosis than insulin-sensitive participants (≥F2: 10% vs. <1%; p<0.001). They also had greater hepatic steatosis, higher ALT, AST, CK-18, HbA1c, and adipose tissue insulin resistance (Adipo-IR) levels, and lower adiponectin concentrations (all p<0.001). Fibrosis was infrequent among insulin-sensitive participants and almost exclusively limited to mild fibrosis (stage F1). Among participants with steatosis, ≥F2 fibrosis was present in 1% of insulin-sensitive participants compared with 13% of insulin-resistant participants (p<0.001). Conclusions Clinically significant fibrosis (≥F2) was uncommon among insulin-sensitive individuals with T2D and largely limited to mild fibrosis (F1). HOMA-IR <2.5 identified a subgroup at very low risk for fibrosis, supporting its potential use as a simple, clinically accessible tool for MASLD risk stratification in primary care and endocrinology settings.

title: Urorectal septum malformation sequence presenting with complete penoscrotal transposition, urethral atresia, and imperforate anus: A case report.
abstract: Urorectal septum malformation sequence (URSMS) is a rare congenital anomaly featuring severe genitourinary and gastrointestinal malformations. We report a neonate with complete URSMS, characterized by complete penoscrotal transposition, a hypoplastic phallus without urethral opening, and an imperforate anus. Laboratory evaluation revealed an elevated serum creatinine of 2.47 mg/dL. Intraoperatively, the rectum and urethra formed a common channel at the phallic base. Anoplasty and urethrostomy were performed. Postoperatively, the infant was anuric and ultrasound confirmed bilateral multicystic dysplastic kidney. Recognition of URSMS is important for accurate diagnosis, surgical planning, and counselling regarding prognosis.

title: Risk-stratified Prostate Cancer Screening in 2026: Blood- and Urine-based Biomarkers.
abstract: Prostate cancer (PCa) encompasses a broad biological spectrum ranging from indolent to aggressive disease. Although early randomized trials generated controversy regarding the benefits versus harms of screening, contemporary evidence supports screening and early detection strategies that focus on men at the highest risk of clinically significant PCa (csPCa) or International Society of Urological Pathology grade group ≥2. Current guidelines from major urological associations emphasize shared decision-making, with earlier screening considerations for high-risk populations. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing is important in PCa screening, but its limited specificity necessitates adjunctive tools to reduce unnecessary biopsies and overdiagnosis. Risk calculators/nomograms, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), blood-based assays (including PSA derivatives and multivariable tests such as the Prostate Health Index, 4Kscore, Stockholm3, and Proclarix), and urine-based assays (including SelectMDx, MyProstateScore 2.0, ExoDx, and miR Sentinel) further refine detection. The integration of MRI and biomarkers represents modern risk-adapted screening and early detection pathways. Ongoing large-scale trials are evaluating multimodal biomarker and MRI strategies to optimize csPCa detection while minimizing harm. Overall, risk-stratified, imaging- and biomarker-driven approaches offer pragmatic and evidence-based pathways to enhance early detection of csPCa while reducing overdiagnosis and overtreatment. PATIENT SUMMARY: This short review discusses how blood and urine tests, alongside genetic risk information, can help identify the men most likely to harbor aggressive prostate cancer-enabling early detection and intervention while avoiding unnecessary biopsies and potential harm in men at low risk.

title: Machine Learning Models Combining [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET Radiomics and Clinical Features to Predict Overall Survival for Metastatic Castration-resistant Prostate Cancer Treated with [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA Radioligand Therapy.
abstract: Purpose Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) remains incurable despite recent therapeutic advances. [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT (lutetium-177 labelled prostate-specific membrane antigen radioligand therapy) provides meaningful clinical benefit in selected patients. However, ∼30% of the patients do not respond to [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT. Although several baseline prognostic factors are well known, reliable pretherapeutic predictive biomarkers are still lacking. We developed and compared several predictive machine learning (ML) models integrating clinical, biochemical, and imaging data, including [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET (gallium-68 labelled prostate-specific membrane antigen ligand positron emission tomography) radiomic features, to estimate overall survival (OS) in patients with mCRPC treated with [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT. Methods This retrospective monocentric study included 102 patients with mCRPC treated with [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA between January 2022 and March 2024. Five lesions per patient were segmented on their pretherapeutic [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET/computed tomography (CT) scans. Radiomic features were extracted following Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative guidelines. Multimodal ML models integrating clinical, genomic, biochemical, and imaging features (including radiomics) were developed to predict OS. Results Median OS of the total cohort was 11.2 mo. Intralesional homogeneity, characterized by the second-order radiomic feature normalized inverse difference moment, was associated with shorter OS (p = 0.025). The best-performing ML model achieved a 12-mo area under the curve (AUC) of 0.778 by combining 22 clinical, biochemical, genomic, and radiomic features. The model leveraging PET data alone achieved strong performance, with an AUC comparable to the clinical model (0.715 vs 0.766). Conclusions ML models based on [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT, including radiomic features, offer a noninvasive, standardized, and widely accessible approach to predict OS in patients with mCRPC treated with [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT. This study highlights the strong predictive potential of PSMA PET imaging for patient stratification in a real-world setting.

title: The Nature of Progression on Active Surveillance for Favorable-risk Gleason Grade Group 2 Prostate Cancer.
abstract: Background Active surveillance (AS) is a recommended option for favorable-risk Gleason grade group 2 (GG2) prostate cancer (PCa), but uptake varies. Objective To describe the nature of progression of confirmed GG2 disease in a well-annotated AS cohort. Design, setting, and participants Participants at the University of California, San Francisco, were diagnosed with cT1-2N0/xM0/x, prostate-specific antigen (PSA) <20 ng/ml, core positivity ≤50%, and GG2 PCa without expansile cribriform or intraductal carcinoma (EC/IDC) at diagnosis, with two or more biopsies on AS from 2000 to 2025. Intervention Active surveillance. Outcome measurements and statistical analysis Outcomes were upgrade (GG3 or higher), volume increase to >50%, EC/IDC, disease progression (upgrade, volume increase, or EC/IDC), active treatment, recurrence (biochemical recurrence or salvage treatment) after radical prostatectomy (RP), metastasis, and PCa-specific mortality (PCSM). Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to identify risk factors for AS outcomes. Results and limitations A total of 329 men were included. At 5 and 10 yr of follow-up, respectively, the upgrade rate was 31% and 58%, volume increase rate was 22% and 31%, EC/IDC development rate was 10% and 41%, disease progression rate was 44% and 79%, active treatment rate was 46% and 65%, and metastasis rate was 0.80% and 3.3%. The 5-yr post-RP recurrence rate was 32%. No PCSM events were recorded within 10 yr. PSA density (PSAD) and positive baseline multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI; Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System 4-5) were associated with disease progression and active treatment. Limitations include the single-institution cohort, a largely Caucasian population, and incomplete mpMRI and genomic testing. Conclusions Men with confirmed favorable-risk GG2 PCa on AS have moderate rates of disease progression requiring treatment at 10 yr. Metastasis and PCSM rates were low, but confidence intervals are wide and require external validation. Positive mpMRI and increased PSAD were associated with disease progression and can help tailor AS intensity.

title: Can We Omit Systematic Biopsies in Men with a Positive MRI During Repeat Biopsies for Active Surveillance for Prostate Cancer? Results from the PRIAS Study.
abstract: Background and objective This study evaluated the added value of systematic biopsies (SBx) in addition to targeted biopsies (TBx) for detecting upgrading during repeat biopsies on active surveillance (AS) using data from the Prostate Cancer Research International Active Surveillance study. Methods We analyzed repeat biopsies of men who underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and SBx at diagnosis, with or without TBx depending on the presence of an MRI lesion, had at least one positive (Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System 3-5) follow-up MRI, and received both SBx + TBx at subsequent repeat biopsy. Upgrading compared with diagnostic biopsy was assessed for TBx only, SBx only, and both, using three definitions: any upgrading, upgrading to grade group (GG) ≥2 with cribriform growth or intraductal carcinoma (≥GG2+), and upgrading to ≥GG3. Cumulative incidences were calculated using each detection method as competing events. For upgrading ≥GG2+ detected by SBx only, the laterality relative to the MRI lesion was determined. Key findings and limitations We analyzed 650 repeat biopsies in 568 patients with a median follow-up of 3.0 yr (interquartile range = 1.8-4.3) for men still on AS. During available follow-up, any upgrading occurred in 238 biopsies (37%), of which 47 (7.2%) were detected by SBx only. Upgrading to ≥GG2+ and ≥GG3 was observed in 100 biopsies (16%) and 78 biopsies (12%), respectively, with SBx alone identifying 19 (3.0%) and 15 (2.3%) of these patients. At 6 yr, the cumulative incidence of ≥GG2+ upgrading was 27% (95% confidence interval [CI] = 21-32%), with 5.4% (95% CI = 2.9-9.1%) for upgrading detected exclusively by SBx. Three of the 19 cases with upgrading to ≥GG2+ detected by SBx only were located contralateral to the MRI lesion (0.5% of all biopsies). Limitations include the retrospective design, which may introduce selection and registration biases. Conclusions and clinical implications In men on AS who underwent diagnostic MRI with SBx (with or without TBx) and a positive follow-up MRI, SBx has limited added value during repeat biopsies, particularly for contralateral sampling, supporting a targeted and perilesional biopsy approach.

title: Malignant transformation of endometriosis into endometrioid ovarian carcinoma with a contralateral borderline seromucinous tumour: A rare case report.
abstract: Background Endometriosis-associated ovarian cancer is uncommon and is most often represented by endometrioid and clear cell carcinomas. Synchronous contralateral borderline ovarian tumours are uncommon and may be missed when gross intraoperative assessment is reassuring. Case A 43-year-old woman with a confirmed diagnosis of endometriosis for approximately 5 years presented with worsening pelvic pain and menstrual symptoms. A left ovarian endometrioma increased from 6.1 × 6.8 × 5.2 cm in April 2024 to 8.8 × 9 × 9.5 cm in April 2025, with subsequent MRI showing a complex mass with solid components (O-RADS MRI 5). CA-125 was 408.6 U/mL and CA 19-9 was 643.58 U/mL; RMI-I was 1225.8 (U = 3, M = 1, CA-125 = 408.6). Staging laparotomy was performed. Histopathology demonstrated grade 2 endometrioid adenocarcinoma arising in an endometriotic cyst of the left ovary, FIGO stage IC1, while the grossly normal-appearing right ovary contained a borderline seromucinous tumour with endometrioid differentiation. The omentum, peritoneal cytology, and all 31 sampled lymph nodes were negative for malignancy. Immunohistochemistry supported endometrioid carcinoma. Conclusion This case highlights the importance of interval change and suspicious imaging features in an endometrioma, the limitations of gross intraoperative assessment of the contralateral ovary, and the value of complete histopathological examination in identifying synchronous bilateral ovarian pathology.

title: 177 Lu-Prostate-specific Membrane Antigen Prior to Stereotactic Ablative Radiotherapy in Oligorecurrent Prostate Cancer: Secondary and Exploratory End Point Results from the Randomized Phase 2 LUNAR Trial.
abstract: The phase 2 randomized LUNAR trial previously demonstrated that neoadjuvant 177 Lu-PNT2002 before stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) in patients with oligorecurrent hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (orHSPC). We report updated efficacy and safety outcomes with extended follow-up. Patients with prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT)-detected orHSPC and one to five metastatic lesions amenable to SBRT were randomized 1:1 to SBRT alone or two cycles of neoadjuvant 177 Lu-PNT2002 followed by SBRT. The primary end point was PFS, defined as new lesions on PSMA PET/CT, initiation of salvage hormonal therapy, or death. Secondary end points included hormonal therapy-free survival (HT-FS) and 24-mo progression-free status. Exploratory end points included polymetastatic PFS (poly-PFS), castration-resistant disease-free survival (CRFS), and conventional imaging progression-free survival (CT-PFS). Between September 2022 and November 2023, 92 patients were randomized to SBRT alone (n = 47) or 177 Lu-PNT2002 plus SBRT (n = 45). title: PSMA-PET/CT-guided Intensification of Radiation Therapy for Prostate Cancer (PSMAgRT): 5-yr Analysis of a Phase 2 Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Background Prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography (PSMA-PET) improves lesion detection, leading to treatment intensification via PSMA-guided radiotherapy (PSMAgRT), but its impact on patient outcomes remains undefined. Objective We evaluated whether PSMAgRT improves failure-free survival (FFS). Design, setting, and participants This phase 2, two-center, open-label randomized trial enrolled patients planned for standard-of-care (SOC) radiotherapy (RT). Intervention Patients were randomized 1:1 to SOC or PSMAgRT to all detected sites across four strata: salvage post-radical prostatectomy (RP), high-risk, oligometastatic, and salvage post-RT. Between 2018 and 2021, 262 patients were randomized (253 treated/analyzed). Outcome measurements and statistical analysis The primary FFS end point (measured from RT completion) comprised prostate-specific antigen (PSA)/radiological progression, next-line therapy, or death. Secondary end points included freedom from biochemical progression (FFBP; PSA rise ≥0.2 ng/ml post-RP or ≥2 ng/ml above nadir in other strata). Prespecified analyses used a one-sided threshold of p 1 < 0.10, whereas post hoc analyses used two-sided p < 0.05 thresholds and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results and limitations Among 253 patients, median follow-up was 66 mo (range 9-91). The 5-yr primary FFS was 66% with PSMAgRT versus 62% in controls (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.80; one-sided 90% CI, upper bound 1.04; p 1 = 0.14). FFBP favored PSMAgRT: 72% versus 65% overall (subdistribution HR [sHR] 0.70, one-sided 90% CI upper bound 0.92; p 1 = 0.048), 81% versus 66% in patients with high-risk disease (sHR 0.54; p 1 = 0.07), and 80% versus 68% in patients in post-RP stratum (sHR 0.54; p 1 = 0.037). In an exploratory, post hoc analysis combining patients with high-risk disease and those in the post-RP stratum, FFBP favored PSMAgRT (sHR 0.54, 95% CI = 0.32-0.91; two-sided p = 0.02). Only one grade ≥3 event was possibly related to dose escalation. Limitations include a phase 2 design with a heterogeneous population. Conclusions Although the primary FFS end point was not met in the overall population, treatment-effect estimates favored PSMAgRT in the high-risk and post-RP strata. These findings provide a meaningful rationale for the target populations currently being evaluated in the definitive phase 3 PATRON trial. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03525288.

title: Dysregulated Retinal DPP10 Expression with Single Cell-based Next Genomic Sequencing Profiling in X-linked Juvenile Retinoschisis.
abstract: X-linked juvenile retinoschisis (XLRS) is a hereditary retinal dystrophy resulting from mutations in the retinoschisin (RS1) gene, which lead to progressive structural abnormalities in the retina and consequent visual impairment. Despite this, the molecular mechanisms through which RS1 mutations induce cell type-specific transcriptional remodeling during disease progression remain inadequately elucidated. To delineate transcriptional changes associated with RS1 mutations, we conducted single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on a CRISPR/Cas9-engineered Rs1 emR209C knock-in mouse model. Integrative analysis with the Mouse Retina Cell Atlas demonstrated that rod photoreceptors exhibited the most significant transcriptional dysregulation among retinal cell types. Notably, dipeptidyl peptidase-like protein 10 (DPP10) was progressively and markedly upregulated, predominantly within photoreceptors, as the disease advanced. These findings were corroborated by immunofluorescence staining, quantitative PCR, and western blot analyses, which confirmed increased retinal DPP10 expression concurrent with a gradual decline in RS1 levels. To explore the functional implications of DPP10 dysregulation, we developed Y79 retinal cell models expressing either wild-type RS1 or the XLRS-associated RS1 R209C variant. Cells expressing the RS1 R209C mutation exhibited elevated DPP10 expression alongside reduced viability. Crucially, siRNA-mediated knockdown of DPP10 partially rescued cell viability and was associated with reduced GRP78/BiP expression in RS1 R209C-expressing cells, supporting potential functional relevance between DPP10 upregulation and mutant RS1-induced cellular stress. Furthermore, circulating DPP10 concentrations were significantly increased in patients with XLRS compared to control subjects. Collectively, these results identify DPP10 as a molecular alteration associated with RS1 mutation and suggest its potential as a circulating biomarker candidate for XLRS.

title: Circulating microRNAs reflect hemorrhagic MRI markers in cerebral amyloid angiopathy.
abstract: Background Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is a major cause of intracerebral hemorrhage in older individuals. Although cerebral microbleeds (CMBs) and cortical superficial siderosis (cSS) aid MRI diagnosis they offer limited pathophysiological insight. MicroRNAs (miRs) regulate microvascular function and may serve as noninvasive biomarkers for distinguishing CAA subtypes and assessing hemorrhagic risk. This study investigated circulating miR profiles in probable CAA and Dutch-type hereditary CAA and examined their relationship with hemorrhagic MRI markers. Methods Small RNA sequencing was performed on plasma from patients with probable CAA (n = 6) and symptomatic D-CAA (n = 6) compared to matched controls. Candidate miRs were validated by qPCR in a validation cohort of probable CAA patients (n = 20) and controls (n = 20). Bioinformatic analyses identified miR-mRNA interactions and pathway enrichment analysis. Correlation and receiver operating characteristic analyses evaluated the association with hemorraghic MRI-markers and the diagnostic performance of circulating plasma miRs. Results Plasma miR-26b and miR-221 were significantly increased in probable CAA. MiR-26b, miR-221, miR-223, and miR-664a correlated with micro- and macrobleeds, with miR-26b showing the highest diagnostic accuracy (AUC 0.745). Target prediction highlighted genes involved in endothelial cell function including CDKN1B, FOXO1 and PTEN, with enrichment of NPAS4- and MECP2-related transcriptional pathways. Conclusion Circulating miRs show potential as biomarkers reflecting hemorrhagic pathology in CAA.

title: Office Hysteroscopic Removal of an IUD-Myoma Composite Using an 18.5 Fr Hysteroscope and Blue Laser in a Postmenopausal Woman with Cervical Atrophy: A No-Anesthesia Approach.
abstract: Objective To study the feasibility and safety of office-based, no-anesthesia, no-dilation hysteroscopic removal of an intrauterine device (IUD)-myoma complex using a blue laser in a postmenopausal woman with severe cervical atrophy. Design Step-by-step video demonstration of the surgical procedure with narrated explanation. Subjects A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman (G2P2, menopause for 7 years) with a 30+ year indwelling T-shaped copper IUD. She had no postmenopausal bleeding or pelvic pain. Examination revealed severe cervical atrophy with marked stenosis. Transvaginal ultrasound (both 2D and 3D) showed the IUD encased by a myoma-like lesion, forming an IUD-myoma complex measuring approximately 2.5 cm × 2.0 cm × 1.8 cm. The patient declined inpatient surgery under anesthesia. Intervention Office vaginoscopic hysteroscopy was performed without anesthesia or cervical dilation using an 18.5 Fr continuous-flow hysteroscope (5 Fr working channel). Normal saline was used as the distension medium at a pressure of 100 mmHg with continuous fluid circulation. A 450 nm blue laser (30 W, continuous mode) was introduced through the working channel to vaporize the myoma-like tissue in a stepwise manner. Once the IUD was fully exposed, 5 Fr grasping forceps were used to remove the IUD together with the remaining myoma tissue en bloc. After vaporization, residual tissue fragments were retrieved for histopathological examination. Main outcome measures Successful IUD removal, operative time, pain score (Visual Analog Scale, VAS 0-10), intraoperative and postoperative complications, and follow-up ultrasound findings at one week. Results The procedure was successfully completed without conversion to general anesthesia or cervical dilation. Total operative time was 36 minutes. The patient tolerated the procedure well, reporting mild discomfort (VAS pain score 3/10). No intraoperative complications occurred. The patient experienced slight vaginal bleeding for 2 days postoperatively, which resolved spontaneously. At the one-week follow-up visit, transvaginal ultrasound revealed a normal uterine cavity with no residual IUD fragments or myoma tissue. Histopathological examination of the residual tissue fragments confirmed benign leiomyoma. Conclusion Office-based, no-anesthesia, no-dilation hysteroscopic removal of an IUD-myoma complex using a blue laser is feasible and safe in a postmenopausal woman with severe cervical atrophy. This technique offers a patient-centered alternative for women at high anesthesia risk or who prefer to avoid hospital admission. To our knowledge, this is the first report of using a blue laser for an IUD-myoma complex under such challenging conditions. Patient consent The patient included in this video gave consent for publication of the video and posting of the video online including social media, the journal website, scientific literature websites (such as PubMed, ScienceDirect, Scopus, etc.) and other applicable sites.

The patient tolerated the procedure well, reporting mild discomfort (VAS pain score 3/10). No intraoperative complications occurred. The patient experienced slight vaginal bleeding for 2 days postoperatively, which resolved spontaneously. At the one-week follow-up visit, transvaginal ultrasound revealed a normal uterine cavity with no residual IUD fragments or myoma tissue. Histopathological examination of the residual tissue fragments confirmed benign leiomyoma.

Conclusion

Office-based, no-anesthesia, no-dilation hysteroscopic removal of an IUD-myoma complex using a blue laser is feasible and safe in a postmenopausal woman with severe cervical atrophy. This technique offers a patient-centered alternative for women at high anesthesia risk or who prefer to avoid hospital admission. To our knowledge, this is the first report of using a blue laser for an IUD-myoma complex under such challenging conditions.

The patient included in this video gave consent for publication of the video and posting of the video online including social media, the journal website, scientific literature websites (such as PubMed, ScienceDirect, Scopus, etc.) and other applicable sites.

title: Joint associations of endometrial thickness and pattern with live birth after fresh and frozen-thawed embryo transfer: a retrospective cohort study of 45,729 cycles.
abstract: Objective To investigate how endometrial thickness and pattern jointly relate to live birth in fresh and frozen-thawed embryo transfer cycles. Design Retrospective cohort study. Subjects A total of 45,729 embryo transfer cycles performed between January 2018 and August 2022, including 16,566 fresh and 29,163 frozen-thawed cycles. Exposure Endometrial thickness and pattern were assessed by transvaginal ultrasound on the trigger day in fresh cycles and on the day of progesterone initiation in frozen-thawed cycles. Fresh and frozen-thawed cycles were analyzed separately. Main outcome measures Live birth per embryo transfer cycle. Results In both fresh and frozen-thawed cycles, restricted cubic spline analyses demonstrated significant overall and nonlinear associations between endometrial thickness and live birth (all P<0.001), while non-A morphology was associated with a lower adjusted live birth risk than type A morphology in no-interaction modified Poisson models (fresh: aRR, 0.880; 95% CI, 0.832-0.930; frozen-thawed: aRR, 0.892; 95% CI, 0.863-0.923). In fresh cycles, type B/C was associated with lower live birth risk than type A within the 7.0-7.9 mm and 8.0-8.9 mm strata. In frozen-thawed cycles, live birth rates increased from 16.7% in the <7 mm B/C group to 44.7% in the ≥14 mm A group, with a significant type A advantage within strata below 10 mm. In some frozen-cycle comparisons, thinner type A endometrium significantly outperformed the adjacent thicker B/C stratum, indicating that type A morphology was associated with higher live birth rates within thinner endometrial strata. Adjusted spline curves showed that live birth risk increased most rapidly at lower thicknesses, with the slope beginning to attenuate at approximately 11-12 mm in fresh cycles and 9-10 mm in frozen-thawed cycles. Sensitivity analyses reproduced the same overall pattern. Additionally, endometrial thickness and morphology varied with ovarian stimulation protocol and gonadotropin duration in fresh cycles, and with endometrial preparation regimen in frozen-thawed cycles. Conclusion Endometrial thickness showed a nonlinear association with live birth, and trilaminar morphology was associated with higher adjusted live birth rates in both fresh and frozen-thawed embryo transfer cycles. The prognostic contribution of endometrial pattern was most evident in thin-to-intermediate endometrium.

title: Ultrasound-assisted enzymatic synthesis of medium- and long-chain triacylglycerols from tricaprylin and algal oil.
abstract: Medium and long-chain triacylglycerols (MLCTs) are functional lipids, but their efficient synthesis in various systems remains challenging. An ultrasound-assisted enzymatic interesterification process was developed using tricaprylin and algal oil as substrates. The optimized enzymatic conditions were obtained by artificial neural network modeling. The structure of enzyme and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) of enzymatic process were both evaluated. The results showed that the MLCT yield reached 69.16%, with Cy-Cy-DHA as the predominant product (28.99%). Only slight structural changes were observed in the enzyme after ultrasound treatment, while the apparent reaction rate constant increased by nearly 2.8-fold and the activation energy decreased. CFD showed that ultrasound improved substrate diffusion and mixing with a lower maximum static pressure than stirring (178 vs. 259 Pa), suggesting MLCT synthesis was enhanced mainly by mass transfer intensification. This study provides valuable insights into mechanisms underlying ultrasound-enhanced enzymatic processes and guides their further scale-up and industrial application.
