title: Automatic 3D TOF-MRA Intracranial Aneurysm Segmentation using SAM-Guided Multi-View Decoding Network.
abstract: Background Deep learning-based aneurysm segmentation using 3D time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography (TOF-MRA) offers promising non-invasive screening, but its accuracy and generalizability remain limited. Purpose To develop a deep learning model for intracranial aneurysm detection and segmentation on MRA, and evaluate its multicenter performance against the digital subtraction angiography (DSA) gold standard and radiologists of varying experience. Materials and methods MRA images from patients suspected of harboring unruptured intracranial aneurysms were retrospectively collected from Jinhua Municipal Central Hospital for model development. An external test set, with DSA as the reference standard, was gathered from Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine. Manual segmentation of cerebral arteries and aneurysms was performed using 3D-Slicer software. Performance was evaluated via Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), sensitivity, and F1-score, and compared against independent clinical evaluations from radiologists with different experience levels. Results The internal dataset comprised 1,560 patients (1,554 aneurysms), including 421 patients (522 aneurysms) for testing. The external test set included 208 patients (224 aneurysms). On the internal test set, the model achieved a lesion-level sensitivity of 86.0% (95% CI: 82.8 - 88.7), a precision of 87.4% (95% CI: 84.2, 90.0), and a DSC of 0.88 (95% CI: 0.84, 0.90). On the independent external test set, the model demonstrated robust generalizability with a sensitivity of 83.4% (95% CI: 75.9, 88.0) and a DSC of 0.84 (95% CI: 0.79, 0.87). The model achieved an overall detection F1-score of 86.7, significantly outperforming junior radiologists (P <.001) and was comparable to mid-level radiologists (P >.05), with an average processing time of approximately 72seconds per exam. Conclusion The proposed deep learning model demonstrated robust multicenter performance for intracranial aneurysm detection and segmentation. Achieving diagnostic accuracy comparable to mid-level radiologists, it holds potential as an efficient assistive tool for MRA interpretation in clinical workflows.

title: Prospective Cardiac MRI study comparing Recovered COVID-19 patients with Recovered Non-COVID-19 Viral Respiratory Infection Patients (R-COVID-CMR).
abstract: Objective Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) has been associated with subclinical myocardial inflammation. Post-COVID-19 infection, there are concerns about subsequent heart failure and persistent myocarditis. It is unknown how COVID-19 infection compares with non-COVID-19 viral infections in terms of myocardial inflammation based on cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) assessment. This prospective longitudinal study aims to determine and compare the extent and severity of myocardial involvement in patients with COVID-19 infection versus non-COVID-19 viral respiratory infections (control). Method Recruited recovered COVID-19 (RCOVID) patients and recovered non-COVID (non-COVID) patients from several hospitals and COVID-19-designated clinic underwent three CMR examinations for functional assessment, native T1, T2, and extracellular volume (ECV) quantification, with corroborating blood markers (NT-proBNP, white cell count, c-reactive protein, lactate dehydrogenase, and high sensitivity cardiac troponin T). CMR scans took place (i) within 2-week of confirmed recovery, (ii) 3-month, and (iii) 12-month post-recovery. Linear mixed model with Bonferroni correction was used for analysis. Results 152 participants were recruited, 112 RCOVID outpatients (mean age: 41.0; 58.9% female) and 40 non-COVID inpatients (mean age:45.0; 37.5% female). Non-COVID infections included influenza virus, rhinovirus/enterovirus, parainfluenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus, and human metapneumovirus. At all three time points, blood results and cardiac function parameters were not significantly different between RCOVID and non-COVID patient groups (p-value not significant). Both patient groups had no significant differences for native T1/T2 values, ECV, late gadolinium enhancement, T2 short tau inversion recovery, and overall fulfilment of the 2018 revised Lake Louise Criteria at each time points. Conclusion In this prospective longitudinal study with CMR examinations, COVID-19 infection does not cause a worse myocardial inflammatory response than non-COVID-19 viral respiratory infection in terms of CMR parameters, and blood markers. Plain english summary During the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) outbreaks, some COVID-19 patients were incidentally found to have inflammation of the muscular layer of the heart. Healthcare professionals were concerned the inflammation will lead to heart not delivering enough blood to meet body demands (ie. heart failure) in the long run. Therefore, we designed this study to better understand the extent and severity of cardiac involvement in patients with COVID-19 by comparing them to patients with other types of viral respiratory infections, such as influenza, which we were more familiar with. We recruited two groups of patients, one group with patients recovered from COVID-19, the other group with patients recovered from other types of viral respiratory infections. For each patient, we arranged three assessments at 2 weeks, 3 months, and 12 months after their recovery respectively. During each assessment, they had blood taken and underwent a cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) scan, a type of medical imaging used for assessment of heart function. 2018 revised Lake Louise Criteria (LLC) is a set of criteria for diagnosis of myocardial inflammation recommended by a group of experts. We compared the two groups of patients at each time point according to LLC, as well as their blood markers and heart function. In our study, we found that COVID-19 infection does not cause a worse heart muscle inflammatory response than other types of viral respiratory infections. This is reassuring as patients with previous COVID-19 infections will likely not develop inflammation of the heart muscle nor develop heart failure.

Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) has been associated with subclinical myocardial inflammation. Post-COVID-19 infection, there are concerns about subsequent heart failure and persistent myocarditis. It is unknown how COVID-19 infection compares with non-COVID-19 viral infections in terms of myocardial inflammation based on cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) assessment. This prospective longitudinal study aims to determine and compare the extent and severity of myocardial involvement in patients with COVID-19 infection versus non-COVID-19 viral respiratory infections (control).

Method

Recruited recovered COVID-19 (RCOVID) patients and recovered non-COVID (non-COVID) patients from several hospitals and COVID-19-designated clinic underwent three CMR examinations for functional assessment, native T1, T2, and extracellular volume (ECV) quantification, with corroborating blood markers (NT-proBNP, white cell count, c-reactive protein, lactate dehydrogenase, and high sensitivity cardiac troponin T). CMR scans took place (i) within 2-week of confirmed recovery, (ii) 3-month, and (iii) 12-month post-recovery. Linear mixed model with Bonferroni correction was used for analysis.

Results

152 participants were recruited, 112 RCOVID outpatients (mean age: 41.0; 58.9% female) and 40 non-COVID inpatients (mean age:45.0; 37.5% female). Non-COVID infections included influenza virus, rhinovirus/enterovirus, parainfluenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus, and human metapneumovirus. At all three time points, blood results and cardiac function parameters were not significantly different between RCOVID and non-COVID patient groups (p-value not significant). Both patient groups had no significant differences for native T1/T2 values, ECV, late gadolinium enhancement, T2 short tau inversion recovery, and overall fulfilment of the 2018 revised Lake Louise Criteria at each time points.

Conclusion

In this prospective longitudinal study with CMR examinations, COVID-19 infection does not cause a worse myocardial inflammatory response than non-COVID-19 viral respiratory infection in terms of CMR parameters, and blood markers.

Plain english summary

During the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) outbreaks, some COVID-19 patients were incidentally found to have inflammation of the muscular layer of the heart. Healthcare professionals were concerned the inflammation will lead to heart not delivering enough blood to meet body demands (ie. heart failure) in the long run. Therefore, we designed this study to better understand the extent and severity of cardiac involvement in patients with COVID-19 by comparing them to patients with other types of viral respiratory infections, such as influenza, which we were more familiar with. We recruited two groups of patients, one group with patients recovered from COVID-19, the other group with patients recovered from other types of viral respiratory infections. For each patient, we arranged three assessments at 2 weeks, 3 months, and 12 months after their recovery respectively. During each assessment, they had blood taken and underwent a cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) scan, a type of medical imaging used for assessment of heart function. 2018 revised Lake Louise Criteria (LLC) is a set of criteria for diagnosis of myocardial inflammation recommended by a group of experts. We compared the two groups of patients at each time point according to LLC, as well as their blood markers and heart function. In our study, we found that COVID-19 infection does not cause a worse heart muscle inflammatory response than other types of viral respiratory infections. This is reassuring as patients with previous COVID-19 infections will likely not develop inflammation of the heart muscle nor develop heart failure.

title: Accelerated 3D Late Gadolinium Enhancement Pulse Sequence with Isotropic Spatial Resolution, Self-Navigation of Respiratory Motion, and Arrhythmia Rejection for Quantification of Left Atrial Fibrosis in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation.
abstract: Background The left atrium (LA) is a thin structure (1.5-2.5mm). Conventional 3D late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) pulse sequences for imaging the LA typically have limited through-plane resolution (2.5-5mm) or prolonged scan times (10-15min), resulting in poor image quality and limited clinical translatability. We sought to develop and test whether a 3D LGE pulse sequence featuring 1.5mm³ isotropic spatial resolution and a predictable scan time of 600 heartbeats can produce diagnostically acceptable image quality at 1.5T for quantification of LA structural remodeling in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). Methods A 3D LGE pulse sequence was developed using gradient-recalled echo (GRE) readout, stack-of-stars k-space sampling with variable density along the partition direction, retrospective arrhythmia rejection, and XD-GRASP reconstruction with self-navigation of respiratory motion. Thirty patients with AF (twenty imaged prior to first-time ablation, ten prior to repeat ablation) and twenty healthy controls were scanned using this pulse sequence. The upper limit of normal image intensity ratio (IIR) was derived from the control group; specifically, 2 standard deviations (SDs) above the mean. Suspected LA fibrosis was quantified by one rater. Two cardiothoracic radiologists independently graded the image quality across three categories (conspicuity, artifacts, noise) using a 5-point Likert scale per category, with a score of 3 considered clinically acceptable. Results The proposed pulse sequence produced diagnostically acceptable image quality scores in all three categories for AF and control cohorts. Retrospective rejection of data acquired during ectopic heartbeats significantly (p<0.05) improved contrast-to-noise ratio (+3.7%) and sharpness (blur metric -3.2%) metrics, albeit at the expense of a significantly reduced signal-to-noise ratio (-4.4%). The upper limit of normal IIR was 1.43. Using this cutoff value to identify suspected LA fibrosis, compared with the control group (2.47 ± 2.24%), the first-time ablation group (7.45 ± 7.38%) was not significantly different (p = 0.14), whereas the repeat ablation group (14.94 ± 13.83%) was significantly different (p < 0.05). Conclusion The proposed pulse sequence produces diagnostically acceptable image quality at 1.5T and provides evidence of LA structural remodeling in AF patients, including greater suspected LA fibrosis burden, relative to control subjects.

title: Visualization of post-STEMI myocardial infarction and microvascular obstruction with non-contrast, free-breathing whole- heart iT 2 prep-IR BOOST.
abstract: Background Clinical adoption of cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) for risk stratification in ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is often limited by long scan times and the requirement for breath-holding and contrast agents. Objectives This study aimed to validate a non-contrast, free-breathing 3D whole-heart T1/T2 CMR method (iT 2 prep-IR BOOST) for rapid assessment of myocardial injury in STEMI patients, hypothesizing that this technique provides promising diagnostic accuracy and quantitative assessment to conventional contrast-enhanced CMR. Methods A free-breathing 3D isotropic whole-heart iT 2 prep-IR BOOST sequence was performed with a scan time of <8minutes. Sixty-four STEMI patients underwent CMR, including iT 2 prep-IR BOOST, clinical T2-STIR, late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and T1/T2 mapping. The diagnostic performance of iT 2 prep-IR BOOST was evaluated against LGE and T2-STIR to assess myocardial infarction (MI), microvascular obstruction (MVO), and edema. Subgroup analyses further investigated the association between MVO detected by iT 2 prep-IR BOOST and left ventricular (LV) remodeling at 1-year follow-up. Results In 60 STEMI patients, the acquisition was completed in 7.2 ± 0.6min as a single free-breathing 3D whole-heart scan. Patient-level analysis showed high sensitivity and specificity for MVO (100.0% / 87.5%) and segmental MVO detection (95.8% / 97.8%). T 2 prep-IR BOOST yielded robust image contrast for MI comparable to LGE, while offering comparable edema visualization to T2-STIR. Volumetric and transmurality quantifications of MVO, MI, and edema showed excellent agreement with reference standards (all r > 0.90, p < 0.001), supported by significant biophysical correlations with native T1/T2 values (p < 0.001). Furthermore, in a 1-year follow-up cohort (n=51), baseline T 2 prep-IR BOOST-derived MVO volume was associated with adverse left ventricular remodeling, showing significant correlations with both ΔLVEDVI (r = 0.305, p = 0.029) and ΔLVESVI (r = 0.293, p = 0.037). Conclusions In this preliminary single-center study, iT 2 prep-IR BOOST showed promising diagnostic performance and close quantitative agreement with conventional LGE and T2-STIR in stable STEMI patients. Further prospective validation in larger, independent, and more heterogeneous cohorts, including patients unable to undergo contrast-enhanced CMR, is required before this technique can be considered an alternative to standard LGE and T2-weighted sequences.

title: Prognostic Value of Late Gadolinium Enhancement Findings in Isolated Left Ventricular Dilatation and Dilated Cardiomyopathy.
abstract: Background Non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) and isolated left ventricular dilatation (ILVD) are defined as left ventricular (LV) dilatation, with reduced or preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), respectively. We aimed to assess the prognostic value of late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) findings, including LGE extent, location, and number of areas to predict all-cause death in ILVD and DCM, separately. Methods Between 2008 and 2021, we conducted a bicentric retrospective study including all consecutive ILVD and DCM patients referred for cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR). The primary outcome was all-cause death. A propensity-score matching was performed to balance characteristics between ILVD and DCM populations. Cox regressions were performed to determine the prognostic value of each LGE feature. Results Of 2,752 patients (age 52±8 years, 56% males), 408 (15%) patients died after a median (interquartile range) follow-up of 9 (7-12) years, including 268 (16%) of 1,668 DCM patients and 140 (13%) of 1,084 ILVD patients. Overall, 737 (27%) patients had LGE, including 472 (28%) of 1,668 DCM patients and 265 (24%) of 1,084 ILVD patients. After propensity-score matching, in ILVD patients with LGE (N=265), the LGE extent (hazard ratio [HR] 1.38, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.06-1.78, p=0.015), multiple LGE areas (HR=3.39, 95% CI: 1.66-6.92, p<0.001), and its septal location (HR=2.68, 95% CI: 1.59-4.52, p<0.001) were strong prognosticators of death after adjustment. Similarly, after propensity-score matching, in DCM patients with LGE (N=277), the LGE extent (HR=1.39, 95% CI: 1.06-1.83, p=0.018), multiple LGE areas (HR=2.70, 95% CI: 1.20-6.08, p=0.017), and its septal location (HR=2.82, 95% CI: 1.47-5.41, p=0.002) were strongly associated with death. The CMR LGE score performed well in participants with LGE (area under the curve [AUC] at 10 years, 0.79 [95% CI: 0.69-0.89]). Conclusions LGE findings were strongly and independently associated with death in both ILVD and DCM patients, with each successive LGE characteristic providing significant incremental prognostic value beyond traditional prognosticators, including LVEF.

title: Multi-center study of CMR versus cardiac catheterization with endomyocardial biopsy for pediatric transplant surveillance: study protocol.
abstract: Notwithstanding advances in post-transplant care, acute allograft rejection (AR) remains the leading cause of mortality in pediatric heart transplant recipients (PHTX). Endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) continues to be the standard of care for AR detection, despite being invasive, costly, and associated with patient discomfort and potential complications. Non-invasive alternatives, including cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) with T1 and T2 parametric mapping and blood biomarkers (BB) such as cell-free DNA (cfDNA) and microRNA (miRNA), have shown promise in the adult transplant population, but their validation in the pediatric transplant population is lacking. The "Predictive Modeling of Acute Rejection in Pediatric Heart Transplant Recipients" (PEACE) study is a prospective, multicenter trial aiming to assess the diagnostic accuracy of CMR and BB in comparison to EMB. The goal of this manuscript is to describe the purpose and experimental protocol of the PEACE study. The PEACE study's overarching hypothesis is that CMR and BB can consistently and accurately detect myocardial abnormalities, potentially guiding the need for EMB. Secondary objectives include cost-analyses of CMR and BB, as well as a biomarker performance evaluation in biopsy-negative, but symptomatic and suspected AR cases. PEACE will enroll PHTX ages 6-25 years, across approximately 20 U.S. pediatric hospitals. All subjects will undergo EMB for surveillance or suspected AR as standard of care. As part of the research protocol, subjects will undergo blood collection for BB prior to the EMB and CMR within 5 days of EMB. Central core labs will conduct blinded analysis for imaging, pathology, and biomarkers to ensure consistent data interpretation. PEACE represents a critical step in reducing reliance on invasive biopsies in the clinical care of PHTX. By validating non-invasive tools in a large, diverse population, the PEACE study could transform AR detection, resulting in improvement of the patient experience and outcomes in this vulnerable population. (Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT07770659, Non-invasive Prediction of EArly Cardiac rEjection (PEACE)).

title: Myocardial Alterations in Major Depressive Disorder with Anxious Distress: Evidence from Oxygenation-Sensitive CMR and Entropy Analysis.
abstract: Background Patients with major depressive disorder with anxious distress (MDD-A) frequently experience cardiovascular symptoms (CVS), which are associated with impaired quality of life and poorer long-term prognosis. This study aimed to quantitatively evaluate myocardial alterations in MDD-A patients using oxygenation-sensitive cardiovascular magnetic resonance (OS-CMR) and mapping-derived entropy analysis, and to explore their associations with CVS as well as the severity of depressive and anxiety symptoms. Methods In this prospective study, 58 consecutively enrolled medication-naïve patients with MDD-A diagnosed according to DSM-5 criteria and 61 healthy controls were included. All participants underwent CMR examinations at 3.0T. Left ventricular (LV) function, native T1 and T2 values, T1-entropy and T2-entropy, LV strain parameters, and oxygenation-sensitive signal intensity change (OS-SI%) were measured and compared between the two groups. Associations between CMR-derived parameters and CVS, anxiety symptom severity, and depressive symptom severity were assessed separately. A p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Compared with healthy controls, patients with MDD-A exhibited significantly higher T1-entropy (8.3 ± 0.3 vs. 7.5 ± 0.3, p < 0.001) and T2-entropy (9.2 ± 0.4 vs. 8.1 ± 0.3, p < 0.001), whereas OS-SI% was significantly lower (11.4 ± 7.5% vs. 14.5 ± 4.5%, p = 0.007). After adjustment for age, sex, smoking status, and heart rate, multivariable regression analyses revealed that OS-SI% was inversely associated with HAMD scores (β = -0.205, p = 0.043) and HAMA scores (β = -0.453, p < 0.001), and inversely associated with CVS (OR= 0.801, p = 0.002). T1-entropy (β = 4.105, p = 0.022) and T2-entropy (β = 2.793, p = 0.042) were positively associated with HAMD scores. Conclusion OS-SI% and mapping-derived myocardial entropy measures may serve as valuable noninvasive imaging biomarkers for assessing early myocardial alterations in patients with MDD-A.

title: The Right Ventricle in Focus: State-of-the-Art CMR Imaging - Challenges, Standards, and Innovations.
abstract: The right ventricle (RV) is recognized as a critical contributor to cardiovascular outcomes. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) has emerged as the reference standard for comprehensive RV assessment, enabling precise evaluation of ventricular volumes, function, flow, and tissue characterization. In this review, we provide a state-of-the-art overview of RV imaging using CMR. We first outline the anatomical and physiological features that distinguish the RV from the left ventricle. Next, we highlight the key technical challenges in imaging the RV, notably its complex geometry, prominent trabeculation, and thin myocardial wall. We then summarize current clinical CMR approaches, including cine imaging for volumetric assessment, phase-contrast techniques for flow quantification, and methods for tissue characterization such as late gadolinium enhancement. Additionally, we discuss advanced and emerging CMR techniques aimed at overcoming current RV imaging limitations, including high-resolution three-dimensional cine imaging, four-dimensional flow imaging, parametric mapping, and novel reconstruction strategies. These innovations hold promise for improving accuracy, reproducibility, and mechanistic insight into RV structure and function. Finally, we review the clinical role of CMR in major RV pathologies, including congenital heart disease, pulmonary hypertension, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, and tricuspid regurgitation. Across these conditions, CMR provides vital diagnostic and prognostic information, with growing evidence supporting its role in guiding clinical management. As technical advancements continue and standardization improves, CMR is poised to transform RV evaluation from a historically challenging endeavor into a precise and impactful component of cardiovascular care.

title: Endovascular stenting of extracranial cervical artery dissections: A two-center study.
abstract: Purpose Extracranial arterial dissections (EAD) are uncommon in the general population but represent a relatively frequent cause of ischemic stroke in young adults. Most EAD have a favorable prognosis and are managed conservatively with antithrombotic therapy, with current guidelines supporting either antiplatelet or anticoagulant treatment. Endovascular stenting is reserved for selected high-risk cases, and this article reports a multicenter experience with this approach and reviews the available literature. Materials and methods Eighty-four EAD patients who underwent stenting were included. A standardized follow-up protocol at 12 months consisting of a clinical neurological assessment accompanied by imaging studies, including either Computed Tomography, Magnetic Resonance Imaging or Digital Subtraction Angiography was adopted. Results In our cohort, most dissections were spontaneous (81 %) and predominantly involved the internal carotid artery (85 %), with acute stroke being the most common indication for stenting. Technical success was achieved in 85.7 % and complications occurred in 10 %. Three patients with initial stent implantation failure underwent successful secondary attempt. No significant predictors of technical success were identified. At discharge, good functional outcome was observed in 83 % of patients and at 12 months most followed patients showed favorable radiological results with high stent patency (86 %) and excellent clinical outcomes (mRS 0-2 in 97 %). Conclusion The results of our study suggest that for selected patients with medical therapy failure or hemodynamic compromise, stenting is a reasonable alternative. Given the limited evidence on indications, safety and efficacy, further randomized studies comparing stenting with medical management are warranted.

title: Basal forebrain glioma: Clinical characteristics and surgical treatment.
abstract: Background Surgical resection of basal forebrain (BFB) gliomas involving the anterior perforated substance (APS) is associated with a high risk of surgical complications due to multiple perforating arteries that traverse this region. Despite these challenges, surgery in this region serves several important purposes, including cytoreduction, histopathological diagnosis, and seizure control. Methods This study included a consecutive series of 67 patients with gliomas either confined to the BFB (13 cases) or extending to adjacent anatomical regions (54 cases) who underwent surgery at the Burdenko Neurosurgery Center between 2016 and 2023. Three main approaches were used: transsylvian, anterior interhemispheric, and supraorbital subfrontal. In 5 cases, the tumor was removed using a microsurgical burr-hole technique. Results BFB tumors were classified according to 2 features: 1) involvement of anatomical regions adjacent to the BFB and 2) localization of the tumor within the BFB: the septal region (S), anterior APS segment (Pa), and posterior APS segment (Pp). Isolated BFB tumors were found in 13 cases (19.4%), including 4 localized to the septal region. Among 59 patients with early postoperative MRI, median EOR was 82%. EOR 70-90% was achieved in 23 of 59 patients (39.0%), and EOR ≥ 90% in 25 of 59 (42.4%). With extension into the Pp segment, EOR ≥ 90% was achieved less often than in the remaining cohort: 8 of 31 (25.8%) versus 17 of 28 (60.7%), respectively (p = 0.009). Postoperatively, hemiparesis developed in 9 patients (13.4%) and speech disturbances in 12 (17.9%), most often because of injury to the lenticulostriate arteries. Hemiparesis resolved in 2 patients, whereas speech disturbances improved in 10 patients and persisted in 2 patients at 3-6 months. Complete seizure control was achieved in 31 of 44 patients (70.4%). Seizure control was better when EOR exceeded 70%. Multivariable Cox models including EOR and WHO grade showed no significant association between EOR and OS or PFS, whereas higher WHO grade was associated with worse OS and PFS. In the sensitivity analysis restricted to WHO grade 2-3 gliomas, greater EOR was associated with better OS (HR per 10% increase, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.29-0.99; p = 0.047), but not with PFS. Conclusions Resection of BFB gliomas is feasible with an acceptable risk of complications and provides effective seizure control. Greater EOR may be associated with better OS in WHO grade 2-3 gliomas. Tumor extension into the posterior portion of APS is associated with an increased risk of surgical morbidity during BFB glioma resection.

Postoperatively, hemiparesis developed in 9 patients (13.4%) and speech disturbances in 12 (17.9%), most often because of injury to the lenticulostriate arteries. Hemiparesis resolved in 2 patients, whereas speech disturbances improved in 10 patients and persisted in 2 patients at 3-6 months. Complete seizure control was achieved in 31 of 44 patients (70.4%). Seizure control was better when EOR exceeded 70%. Multivariable Cox models including EOR and WHO grade showed no significant association between EOR and OS or PFS, whereas higher WHO grade was associated with worse OS and PFS. In the sensitivity analysis restricted to WHO grade 2-3 gliomas, greater EOR was associated with better OS (HR per 10% increase, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.29-0.99; p = 0.047), but not with PFS.

Conclusions

Resection of BFB gliomas is feasible with an acceptable risk of complications and provides effective seizure control. Greater EOR may be associated with better OS in WHO grade 2-3 gliomas. Tumor extension into the posterior portion of APS is associated with an increased risk of surgical morbidity during BFB glioma resection.

title: Implementation and early experience with tubular retractor-assisted minimally invasive parafascicular surgery for deep brain tumors.
abstract: Minimally invasive parafascicular surgery using tubular retractors (tr-MIPS) has emerged as a strategy to access deep intra-axial lesions while minimizing white matter disruption. However, practical guidance on institutional implementation and integration with modern intraoperative adjuncts remains limited. We describe our early institutional experience with tr-MIPS, with a focus on workflow adoption, multimodal adjunct integration, and feasibility. Demographic, radiographic, operative, and postoperative data were collected, with particular attention to extent of resection, neurological outcomes, and use of adjunctive technologies. Six patients underwent tr-MIPS for deep intra-axial tumors of varied histology. Gross or near-total resection was achieved in four cases. Five patients experienced no new postoperative neurological deficits, and one had transient dysphasia. Median length of stay was 3.5 days. A range of adjuncts including diffusion tensor imaging, 5-aminolevulinic acid fluorescence, intraoperative neurophysiologic monitoring, and depth-electrode electroencephalography were successfully incorporated without workflow disruption. Notably, intraoperative depth-electrode EEG was used to guide resection of an epileptogenic lesion, representing a novel adjunctive application in the tr-MIPS setting. tr-MIPS can be implemented within a modern neurosurgical practice and feasibly integrated with multiple intraoperative adjuncts. We demonstrate feasibility with the addition of this technique to our center's armamentarium. Beyond facilitating access to deep lesions, its compatibility with technologies such as tractography, neurophysiologic monitoring, and EEG expands its functional utility. These findings support the feasibility of a broader adoption of tr-MIPS and highlight opportunities for multimodal, precision-guided minimally invasive neuro-oncologic surgery.

title: Comparing Diagnostic Ability of Two Off-the-Shelf Large Language Models with That of Endodontists for Teeth Requiring Initial Root Canal Treatment: A Multicenter Retrospective Investigation.
abstract: Introduction Despite growing interest in large language models (LLMs) for endodontic diagnosis, prior studies have used simulated cases, examination formats, or small selected series. This multicenter retrospective study compared the diagnostic accuracy of ChatGPT-5.2 and Gemini 3.0 with that of calibrated endodontists across 645 teeth requiring initial root canal treatment. Methods Cases were evaluated across four endpoints: pulpal diagnosis, periapical diagnosis, treatment planning, and case difficulty. Standardized clinical summaries and radiographs were submitted to endodontists and both LLMs using a fixed single-pass protocol. Exact-match accuracy, Cohen's κ, Gwet's AC1, macro-averaged F1 score, McNemar tests, and generalized estimating equations were used for statistical comparison. Results Endpoint accuracies ranged from 74% to 88%. Macro F1 was highest for periapical diagnosis (ChatGPT-5.2, 0.724; Gemini 3.0, 0.719) and lowest for treatment planning (0.385; 0.550), where both models showed lower observed performance in minority categories, interpreted as suggestive given small subgroup sizes. Composite accuracy across the three clinical endpoints was 61.1% (95% CI, 57.4%-64.8%) and 59.4% (95% CI, 55.3%-63.3%), and four-endpoint accuracy was 47.3% (95% CI, 43.3%-51.2%) and 46.2% (95% CI, 42.3%-49.8%), indicating at least one clinically relevant error in about half of cases. Treatment planning was the only endpoint differing between models after Holm-Bonferroni correction, favoring Gemini 3.0 (OR, 1.457; adjusted p = .003). Conclusions Both models performed acceptably on individual endpoints and common presentations, but performance was endpoint-specific and substantially reduced on integrated assessment and low-prevalence categories. These findings support use of LLMs in endodontic diagnosis and treatment planning as adjunctive tools, but not without expert supervision.

title: ASSESSMENT OF TREATMENT RESPONSE RESPONSE AND THE ROLE OF COMPLETION SURGERY AFTER CONCURRENT CRTAND BRACHYTHERAPY FOR LOCALLY ADVANCED CERVICAL CANCER - A REVIEW FROM THE FRENCH CERVICAL CANCER GUIDELINES GROUP.
abstract: Concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT) followed by brachytherapy is the standard of care for locally advanced cervical cancer. However, post-treatment management remains challenging. Accurate response assessment is essential because it informs subsequent management, particularly the indication for completion surgery. Radiation-induced tissue changes may impair the reliability of clinical examination and conventional imaging, while the respective roles of advanced imaging modalities and completion surgery remain debated. Functional lumbopelvic MRI incorporating diffusion-weighted and perfusion sequences is the reference imaging modality for response assessment and provides greater diagnostic performance than clinical examination alone. FDG PET-CT offers complementary information, particularly regarding nodal disease and early metabolic response, but the routine combination of FDG PET-CT with MRI has not been shown to improve diagnostic accuracy. MRI performed early during CRT may help differentiate responders from nonresponders based on changes in the apparent diffusion coefficient. However, the optimal timing of MRI after treatment completion remains uncertain. Available evidence does not support the routine use of conization for response assessment. Completion surgery provides no prognostic benefit and increases morbidity in patients with squamous cell carcinoma who achieve a complete response after CRT and brachytherapy. Evidence remains insufficient to establish its role in adenocarcinoma. When completion surgery is indicated, delaying the procedure until at least 6-8 weeks after CRT may reduce postoperative morbidity. Simple hysterectomy should be favored over radical hysterectomy, which increases morbidity without improving survival. Current evidence demonstrates no superiority of minimally invasive surgery or laparotomy in terms of oncologic outcomes or overall morbidity.

title: Accuracy of Diagnostic Methods for Peripheral Trigeminal Nerve Injuries: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Background Post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathy following oral and maxillofacial procedures may cause persistent neurosensory disturbances and neuropathic pain, yet the diagnostic performance of the available assessment methods remains uncertain. Purpose This systematic review evaluated the accuracy of diagnostic methods used to detect peripheral trigeminal nerve injuries in the maxillary and mandibular regions after oral and maxillofacial procedures. Study selection PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane databases were searched in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines. Diagnostic accuracy and observational studies evaluating clinical, neurophysiological, or imaging-based methods for peripheral trigeminal nerve injuries were included, while non-English and nonhuman studies, reports lacking relevant diagnostic performance data, studies outside the maxillary or mandibular regions, and nonoriginal research were excluded. Risk of bias was assessed using Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2. Results The search identified 2914 records, of which 10 studies (0.3%) were included in the final synthesis, comprising n = 520 participants and k = 514 injured or evaluated nerves. The included studies comprised 5 prospective diagnostic accuracy studies, 2 retrospective diagnostic accuracy studies, 2 case-control diagnostic accuracy studies, and one cross-sectional observational study. Clinical neurosensory testing showed 96% accuracy, 100% sensitivity, 62.5% specificity, 95% positive predictive value (PPV), and 100% negative predictive value (NPV) for lingual nerve (LN) injuries, compared with 73% accuracy, 85% sensitivity, 47% specificity, 77% PPV, and 60% NPV for inferior alveolar nerve injuries. The tongue somatosensory evoked magnetic field laterality index showed 95.7% accuracy, 92.3% sensitivity, 100% specificity, 100% PPV, and 90.9% NPV for LN injury. Conclusions and relevance Clinical neurosensory testing was widely used but had variable diagnostic performance, with lower values for inferior alveolar nerve injuries. Quantitative sensory testing and neurophysiological methods provided more balanced diagnostic profiles, especially when combined. Magnetic resonance neurography demonstrated high specificity but variable sensitivity, with greater clinical value for high-fgrade injuries. The highest single-test accuracy was reported for tongue somatosensory evoked magnetic fields in LN injury. Overall, these findings support a multimodal diagnostic approach when objective confirmation, injury grading, anatomical localization, or treatment planning is required.

title: Computed Tomogrpahy-Guided Management of High-Risk Mandibular Third Molars: A Prospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Background Coronectomy is used to reduce the risk of inferior alveolar nerve (IAN) injury in high-risk mandibular third molars, but comparative studies rarely account for preoperative risk stratification. Purpose To compare postoperative outcomes following coronectomy and complete removal in a computed tomography (CT)-guided, risk-adapted treatment pathway. Study design, setting, and sample This prospective cohort study included consecutive patients with high-risk mandibular third molars treated at Amstelland Hospital, Amstelveen, the Netherlands (2019-2025). All subjects underwent CT assessment after panoramic radiography. Subjects aged < 18 years or with previous surgery, incomplete records, inability to complete follow up, American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status > III, or acute infection were excluded. Predictor variable Planned treatment modality (coronectomy vs complete removal). Main outcome variables The primary outcome was postoperative IAN or lingual nerve sensory disturbance. Secondary outcomes included postoperative complications and treatment-related outcomes, including successful coronectomy, intraoperative conversion to complete removal, and subsequent interventions involving retained roots. Covariates Age, sex, smoking status, American Society of Anesthesiologists classification, impaction classification, and pathology. title: How to Determine the Correct Intraoperative Disc Position in Arthroscopic Temporomandibular Joint Discopexy?
abstract: Background Arthroscopic discopexy has become an increasingly used technique for the treatment of symptomatic disc displacement. However, intraoperative assessment of correct disc position is commonly based on roofing evaluation, which may lead to misinterpretation. Purpose To describe an objective intraoperative method for determining correct disc position during arthroscopic discopexy and measure its association with disc position on immediate postoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Study design, setting, sample Prospective cohort study conducted at a tertiary referral center (Clinica Bupa Santiago). Consecutive patients with symptomatic disc displacement treated between 2024 and 2026 using the mattress-loop technique (Yang technique) were included. Exclusion criteria were incomplete preoperative clinical data and absence of preoperative or immediate postoperative MRI. Predictor variable The primary predictor variable was intraoperative disc position, defined by the relationship between the anterior synovectomy margin and the articular eminence, and categorized as reduced or displaced. Main outcome variable The primary outcome variable was disc position on immediate postoperative MRI, categorized as reduced or displaced. Disc position was assessed using the three-circle method. Covariates Covariates included demographic variables, clinical variables (duration of symptoms, prior nonsurgical treatment, bruxism, joint noise), and imaging variables (disc reduction status, disc morphology, osteoarthritis, effusion, Wilkes stage, disc perforation). Analyses Descriptive statistics were used. Continuous variables are reported as mean (SD) or median (interquartile range), and categorical variables as n (%). Associations were tested using Fisher exact and Mann-Whitney U tests. Joint-level analyses used mixed-effects logistic regression with a random intercept for patient. P < .05 was considered statistically significant. Results A total of 131 subjects comprising 209 temporomandibular joints were included. The median age was 23 years (interquartile range 18), and 120 (91.6%) were female. Intraoperative assessment classified all joints as reduced, whereas immediate postoperative MRI confirmed disc reduction in 207 of 209 joints (99.0%). The association between intraoperative assessment and postoperative disc position was statistically significant (P < .001). Conclusions and relevance An intraoperative assessment method based on the relationship between the anterior synovectomy margin and the articular eminence showed high concordance with immediate postoperative MRI findings. These findings support its potential as an objective intraoperative reference for disc positioning during arthroscopic temporomandibular joint surgery.

title: Tumor-induced osteomalacia caused by a mandibular phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor misdiagnosed as giant cell reparative granuloma: case report.
abstract: Tumor-induced osteomalacia (TIO) is a rare syndrome caused by FGF23-secreting phosphaturic mesenchymal tumors (PMTs). Clinicians frequently misdiagnose mandibular PMTs due to their histological mimicry of giant cell lesions. We report a 16-year-old female with mandibular PMT-induced TIO who endured a 5-year diagnostic delay across eight hospitals. Two factors confounded her diagnosis: histological mimicry of giant cell reparative granuloma and an incidental SMARCAL1 variant misdirecting clinical attention toward a genetic disorder. Ultimately, integrated histopathologic evaluation and focal FGF23 immunohistochemistry supported the diagnosis of PMT, with serum P1NP reaching 435.00 ng/mL and β-CTX exceeding 6.00 ng/mL at peak disease severity, while ¹⁸F-AlF-NOTA-TATE PET/CT localized the lesion. Tumor resection with fibula free flap reconstruction achieved early postoperative improvement in serum phosphate levels and symptoms, although long-term clinical, biochemical, and radiographic follow-up remains necessary to assess durable remission and monitor for recurrence. This case illustrates multiple diagnostic pitfalls in TIO with mandibular PMT, emphasizing that a high index of suspicion and integration of biochemical, histological, and imaging findings are essential to avoid delayed diagnosis.

title: Large Osseous Choristoma of the Tongue Base: A Case Report and Literature Review.
abstract: Osseous choristoma is a rare benign lesion composed of mature bone in an ectopic soft-tissue site, most often the posterior tongue. We report a 9-year-old girl with a 1-year history of a slowly enlarging tongue-base lesion causing dysphagia and snoring during sleep. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography showed a well-circumscribed, homogeneous bony-density lesion measuring 4.0 × 3.8 × 4.1 cm without enhancement or adjacent soft-tissue invasion. The lesion was completely excised through a dorsal tongue approach. Histopathological examination demonstrated mature osseous tissue with bony trabeculae and marrow cavities, confirming osseous choristoma. Recovery was uneventful, with no clinical recurrence at 3 months. Large tongue-base osseous choristomas may cause functional symptoms despite their benign nature. Computed tomography provides a useful diagnostic clue, while definitive diagnosis depends on histopathology. Complete surgical excision remains the treatment of choice.

title: Diagnostic Value of Tc-99m-HDP SPECT/CT in Temporomandibular Joint Osteoarthritis: Correlation with Clinical and Structural Findings.
abstract: Background This study evaluated the diagnostic utility of quantitative Tc-99m-hydroxydiphosphonate (HDP) bone single-photon emission computed tomography/computed tomography (SPECT/CT) in temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis (TMJ OA) by analyzing correlations among tracer uptake, clinical features, and structural imaging to detect early metabolically active disease. Methods A retrospective review included 48 patients (96 TMJs) with TMJ discomfort who underwent SPECT/CT and conventional imaging. Clinical parameters included pain duration, visual analog scale (VAS) score, joint sounds, mandibular range of motion, and occlusal findings. Radiography assessed condylar morphology and cortical erosion, and a Destructive Change Index (DCI) quantified bony changes. SPECT/CT uptake was expressed as maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax). Correlation and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were performed. Results SPECT/CT uptake strongly correlated with condylar cortical erosion on CT (r = 0.80) and moderately with lateral pole tenderness (r = 0.51) and pain VAS score (r = 0.40). Joint sounds and condylar morphology correlated weakly (r = 0.26 and 0.21, respectively), while other clinical factors had negligible associations. ROC analysis identified an optimal SUVmax cutoff of 3.88, yielding 91% sensitivity (95% CI: 80-97%) and 85% specificity (95% CI: 73-94%) for detecting cortical erosion. SPECT/CT revealed increased metabolic uptake in some radiographically normal joints, suggesting the possibility of early osteoarthritic change before overt structural abnormalities became apparent. Conclusion Quantitative SPECT/CT provides complementary metabolic information beyond structural imaging and may facilitate the detection of metabolically active TMJ osteoarthritis.

title: Digital volumetric planning and mixed reality-guided anterolateral thigh flap reconstruction for maxillary defects.
abstract: Background Accurate restoration of soft-tissue volume remains challenging in maxillary reconstruction. This study assessed the feasibility of a defect-oriented digital volumetric planning workflow combined with mixed reality (MR)-guided anterolateral thigh flap (ALTF) harvest. Methods Patients who underwent maxillectomy followed by ALTF reconstruction between November 2023 and January 2025 were retrospectively reviewed. Preoperative CT data were imported into Mimics Medical 21.0 for three-dimensional reconstruction of the maxilla and tumor. Virtual osteotomy and defect simulation were performed to calculate the simulated recipient-defect capacity, designated as V1. Flap dimensions were then designed using V1 and donor-site adipose thickness. MR guidance was used intraoperatively for perforator localization and flap harvest. Intraoperative flap volume was measured by water displacement (V2), and postoperative flap volume was quantified on CT imaging (V3). Secondary outcomes included flap utilization rate, complications, speech intelligibility, patient satisfaction, and University of Washington Quality of Life scores.The three related volumes were compared using the Friedman test, followed by Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons. Results Fifteen patients were included. Mean flap thickness was 10.80 ± 3.49 mm. Median V1, V2, and V3 values were 61.57 mL (interquartile range [IQR], 44.53), 75.00 mL (IQR, 52.00), and 64.26 mL (IQR, 40.65), respectively. The overall difference was significant (Friedman statistic = 17.200, degrees of freedom = 2; P < 0.001). V2 was significantly greater than V1 (adjusted P < 0.001) and V3 (adjusted P = 0.003), whereas V1 and V3 did not differ significantly (adjusted P = 1.000). Mean flap utilization rate was 91.13 ± 9.67%. All flaps survived. One patient developed titanium mesh exposure after radiotherapy; no other major complications occurred. Postoperative speech intelligibility and quality-of-life outcomes were generally favorable. Conclusions Digital volumetric planning combined with MR-guided ALTF harvest was technically feasible in this preliminary cohort and provided a reference for individualized flap design. The findings should be interpreted as exploratory, and comparative studies with larger samples are needed to determine whether this workflow improves clinical outcomes or reduces tissue trimming.

title: Prognostic factors in patients with lower gingival squamous cell carcinoma by computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging: an especial focus on mandibular canal invasion and masticator space invasion.
abstract: Introduction The study aimed to research the prognostic factors in patients with lower gingival squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) by computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), especially focus on mandibular canal invasion and masticator space invasion. Material & methods Forty-eight patients with lower gingival SCC underwent CT and MRI for pre-treatment. The prognostic factors were assessed by chi-square test with the Fisher's exact test. The five-year overall survival rates were analyzed by Kaplan-Meier method with log rank test. Results The results demonstrated that masticator space invasion with MRI was significant predictive variable for regional lymph node metastasis (p = 0.015), and that bone invasion with CT, masticator space invasion with MRI and T-primary tumour (TNM classification 9th Edition) were significant predictive variables for survival (p < 0.001, p = 0.004 and p < 0.001, respectively). The five-year overall survival rate in bone invasion with CT was 77.1 % for non-mandibular canal invasion and 0 % for mandibular canal invasion, respectively (p < 0.001). The five-year overall survival rate in masticator space invasion with MRI was 68.8 % for no invasion and 12.5 % for masticator space invasion, respectively (p < 0.001). Furthermore, the five-year overall survival rate in T-primary tumour was 80.9 % for T1-3 and 7.1 % for T4, respectively (p < 0.001). Conclusion This study suggested that the mandibular canal invasion with CT may be a potential prognostic factor and that further multicenter validation is needed.

The results demonstrated that masticator space invasion with MRI was significant predictive variable for regional lymph node metastasis (p = 0.015), and that bone invasion with CT, masticator space invasion with MRI and T-primary tumour (TNM classification 9th Edition) were significant predictive variables for survival (p < 0.001, p = 0.004 and p < 0.001, respectively). The five-year overall survival rate in bone invasion with CT was 77.1 % for non-mandibular canal invasion and 0 % for mandibular canal invasion, respectively (p < 0.001). The five-year overall survival rate in masticator space invasion with MRI was 68.8 % for no invasion and 12.5 % for masticator space invasion, respectively (p < 0.001). Furthermore, the five-year overall survival rate in T-primary tumour was 80.9 % for T1-3 and 7.1 % for T4, respectively (p < 0.001).

Conclusion

This study suggested that the mandibular canal invasion with CT may be a potential prognostic factor and that further multicenter validation is needed.

title: Procedure-specific cranial base responses after surgically assisted rapid palatal expansion and Le Fort I osteotomy.
abstract: Background The biological effects of maxillary surgery may extend beyond the operative site to involve the posterior cranial base. Although biomechanical studies have suggested force transmission to the spheno-occipital synchondrosis (SOS), procedure-specific cranial base responses have not previously been quantitatively evaluated using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)-based radiomics. Objective To compare postoperative cranial base responses following surgically assisted rapid palatal expansion (SARPE) and Le Fort I osteotomy by quantitatively evaluating the SOS using CBCT-based radiomics. Materials and methods This retrospective observational study included 25 skeletally mature patients treated with either SARPE (n = 12) or Le Fort I osteotomy (n = 13). Preoperative and three-month postoperative CBCT scans were analyzed. The SOS was manually segmented using a standardized anatomical reference framework, and 107 radiomic features were extracted according to Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative recommendations. Within-group and between-group comparisons were performed using non-parametric tests with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction. Selected radiomic features were further analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. Results Radiographic SOS separation rates were comparable between the SARPE and Le Fort I groups (p > 0.05). Following false discovery rate correction, 43 radiomic features demonstrated significant postoperative alterations in the SARPE group, whereas four features showed nominally significant changes after Le Fort I osteotomy (p < 0.05), none of which remained significant after FDR correction. Nominal between-group comparisons identified four features with p < 0.05, but none remained significant after FDR correction. Linear mixed-effects analysis identified a significant Group × Time interaction for GLSZM Large Area Low Gray Level Emphasis (FDR-adjusted p = 0.024), supporting a procedure-specific longitudinal response. Heatmap and volcano plot analyzes demonstrated a broader distribution of postoperative imaging-derived changes following SARPE than after Le Fort I osteotomy. Conclusions SARPE and Le Fort I osteotomy produced distinct postoperative responses within the spheno-occipital synchondrosis, suggesting that cranial base adaptation varies according to the surgical procedure. The broader radiomic response observed following SARPE is consistent with the hypothesis that preservation of the pterygomaxillary connection may permit greater force transmission to the posterior cranial base. CBCT-based radiomics may provide a sensitive quantitative method for characterizing procedure-specific cranial base responses.

title: Comparison of the efficacy of three-dimensional printing-assisted strategy and traditional total ankle arthroplasty in the treatment of end-stage ankle arthritis.
abstract: Objective To compare perioperative parameters, early functional outcomes, and complication profiles between 3D printing-assisted total ankle arthroplasty strategy incorporating preoperative virtual planning, patient-specific osteotomy guides, and a customized talar component and conventional total ankle arthroplasty (TAA) in the treatment of end-stage ankle arthritis. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on data from 44 patients diagnosed with end-stage ankle arthritis who were admitted to our hospital between January 2021 and December 2023. Among them, 20 patients (observation group) underwent total ankle arthroplasty (TAA) using a 3D-printed patient-specific TAA strategy, while 24 patients (control group) received conventional TAA using the same tibial component and polyethylene liner but a standard off-the-shelf talar component, together with standard instrumentation. The following parameters were recorded and evaluated: operative duration, intraoperative blood loss, length of postoperative hospital stay, intraoperative fluoroscopy time, preoperative and postoperative American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS) scores, visual analogue scale (VAS) scores, and ankle range of motion (ROM). Additionally, the occurrence of soft tissue-related complications was monitored. Results The AOFAS score, VAS score, and ankle range of motion (ROM) in both groups showed significant improvement postoperatively compared to preoperative values (P < 0.05). However, no statistically significant differences were observed between the two groups (P > 0.05). With regard to surgical outcomes, including operative time, intraoperative blood loss, postoperative hospitalization duration, and the intraoperative fluoroscopy time, the observation group demonstrated significantly better results than the control group (P < 0.001). Concerning postoperative complications, the observation group experienced only one case of superficial infection, whereas the control group had two cases of superficial infection and one case of wound edge necrosis. Although the total complication rate was slightly lower in the observation group, the difference between the two groups was not statistically significant (P = 0.389). Postoperative radiographic analysis confirmed significantly improved alignment accuracy of the tibial component in the observation group compared to the control group (P < 0.05). Conclusion The 3D printing-assisted TAA strategy appears to improve perioperative efficiency and short-term radiographic alignment accuracy compared with conventional TAA, whereas short-term functional outcomes and wound-related complication rates remain comparable between groups. Given the additional preoperative preparation time and cost, its theoretical promise for patients with complex deformities and its potential effect on long-term implant survival require further confirmation through prospective, randomized studies with long-term follow-up.

title: Multimodal photoacoustic arthroscopy for quantitative morphomechanical assessment of articular cartilage.
abstract: Background Osteoarthritis (OA) involves progressive cartilage degeneration, while conventional white-light arthroscopy mainly provides surface morphological information and lacks quantitative functional contrast. Multimodal photoacoustic arthroscopy (MMPA) may strengthen intraoperative cartilage assessment by enabling earlier identification of matrix, collagen, and biomechanical alterations that are not readily visible under white light. Methods We developed a preclinical multimodal photoacoustic arthroscopy (MMPA) prototype integrating photoacoustic imaging, polarization-resolved photoacoustic imaging, and photoacoustic elasticity imaging to enable label-free, in situ microscopic-resolution assessment of cartilage composition, collagen-related structural anisotropy, and biomechanical response. Validation was performed on 300 human cartilage regions spanning multiple degenerative grades. A feature-based machine-learning classifier was developed mainly using cartilage regions with Mankin scores from 2 to 9, and an independent external validation cohort including 120 cartilage regions was used to assess model generalizability. Longitudinal in vivo monitoring was conducted in a large-animal model. MRI and white-light arthroscopy were used as comparative imaging modalities, whereas histopathological grading served as the reference standard. Results MMPA provided additional visualization of microscopic morphomechanical changes that were less apparent on conventional white-light arthroscopy. The multimodal machine-learning model achieved AUCs of 0.93 (95% CI: 0.91-0.95) internally and 0.89 (95% CI: 0.87-0.90) externally. MMPA detected 81% of lesions, compared with 78% for MRI and 72% for white-light arthroscopy, with a significant overall difference (Cochran's Q=21.00 , p=2.75×10-5 ) and significant pairwise differences (MMPA vs MRI, p=0.0313 ; MMPA vs white-light arthroscopy, p=0.000831 ). MMPA-derived scores most closely tracked histopathological severity. Conclusion This study establishes a preclinical multimodal photoacoustic arthroscopy framework for quantitative intraoperative morphomechanical assessment of articular cartilage degeneration. MMPA has potential to serve as a quantitative upgrade to conventional white-light arthroscopy, assisting surgeons in earlier recognition of degenerative cartilage changes from Mankin score 2 onward, lesion evaluation, and intraoperative decision-making. The translational potential of this article : This study presents a preclinical multimodal photoacoustic arthroscopy platform that provides quantitative intraoperative assessment of cartilage composition, structural anisotropy, and biomechanical properties. Rather than replacing MRI, MMPA is intended to complement preoperative MRI by offering real-time functional assessment during arthroscopy.

title: Somatic Growth Faltering Precedes Brain Growth Deceleration in Preterm Infants: A Window for Intervention.
abstract: Objective To identify the timing and clinical risk factors associated with somatic growth faltering (GF) in very preterm infants (VPI, born < 32 weeks' gestation) and explore the relationship with longitudinal brain growth throughout the extrauterine second and third trimesters. Study design Observational cohort followed with serial growth anthropometrics and brain magnetic resonance imaging at approximately 4-week intervals through term corrected age. Multivariable logistic regression identified clinical covariates associated with GF. Generalized additive models, extended linear mixed models, and multivariable linear mixed models were applied to create trajectories of nutritional intake and weight and brain growth and compare term corrected brain volumes between VPI with and without GF. Results 118 VPI (68 GF, 50 no GF) underwent 333 magnetic resonance imaging studies (195 GF, 138 no GF). Those with GF were born younger (mean [SD] 27.4 [2.2] vs 28.3 [2.3] weeks, p=0.02) and experienced more clinical comorbidities. Poor weight gain in GF VPI began after 33 weeks corrected age and was associated with early systemic steroids (odds ratio [95% CI] 3.8 [1.2,14.8], P=0.03) and gastrointestinal surgery (odds ratio [95% CI] 7.8 [1.8,53.9], P=0.01). GF infants demonstrated significantly lower lipid, caloric, and maternal milk intake trajectories than non-GF infants. VPI with GF compared with no GF experienced slower volumetric brain growth after 37 weeks corrected age in nearly all brain regions. Term corrected cerebellar (β= -1.74 [-2.95,-0.52], p=0.01) and brainstem (β= -0.29 [-0.55,-0.04], p=0.02) volumes were lower in GF infants after adjusting for significant covariates. Conclusions Brain growth is impaired during critical extrauterine periods in GF VPI, with a 4-week interval between the onset of weight faltering and subsequent brain growth deceleration that may represent an important window for clinical intervention.

title: Surgery-first versus endoscopy-first for pediatric choledocholithiasis: Systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Background The incidence of pediatric choledocholithiasis is rising, yet the optimal initial treatment strategy remains debated. Clinicians must choose between an endoscopy-first approach (preoperative ERCP followed by laparoscopic cholecystectomy) and a surgery-first strategy (laparoscopic cholecystectomy with intraoperative cholangiography and bile duct exploration). Direct pediatric data comparing these two strategies remain scarce, and clinical decision-making therefore continues to rely heavily on evidence extrapolated from adult populations. Methods We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies comparing surgery-first versus endoscopy-first management of pediatric choledocholithiasis, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane databases were searched from inception to December 2025. title: VIRTUAL REALITY-ENHANCED FOR PREOPERATIVE ANATOMICAL ASSESSMENT OF ABDOMINAL NEUROBLASTOMA: A COMPARATIVE STUDY WITH CONVENTIONAL CT IMAGING.
abstract: Aim Accurate assessment of tumour anatomy is critical for neuroblastoma surgical planning. This study evaluated whether patient-specific virtual reality (VR) models improve the accuracy of pre-operative anatomical assessment compared with conventional computed tomography (CT) imaging. Methods CT scans from nine patients with abdominal neuroblastoma were segmented to create patient-specific VR models, which were then imported into an in-house VR application. Eleven paediatric surgeons (n=5 consultants; n=6 registrars) independently evaluated conventional CT images and VR reconstructions to assess vascular and organ involvement, image-defined risk factors (IDRFs), and operative strategies. Anatomical accuracy was quantified against intraoperative findings recorded in the International Neuroblastoma Surgical Report Form. Subjective ratings were collected using Likert scales. Mixed-effects models and non-parametric statistical analyses were conducted (p<0.05). Results VR significantly improved overall anatomical accuracy, with a mean increase of 12.4 percentage points (95% CI 8.5-16.3; p<0.0001). Improvements were observed for vascular involvement (+12.5%, p<0.001), organ involvement (+9.6%, p<0.01), and IDRF identification (+13.7%, p<0.0001). Improvements in anatomical accuracy with VR were similar between consultants and registrars. VR did not significantly alter operative planning decisions or predicted tumour resectability. Surgeons reported greater confidence in anatomical understanding and surgical planning with VR than CT (p<0.001). The VR platform received high ratings for usability, integration into the preoperative planning workflow, and perceived clinical value. Conclusion VR improved surgeons' anatomical assessment accuracy and confidence compared with traditional CT scans, highlighting VR's potential as a useful supplement to conventional imaging for preoperative evaluation in complex abdominal neuroblastoma.

title: Unfolding new horizons: Machine learning applications for pediatric intussusception - A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Background Pediatric intussusception is among the most common surgical emergencies in early childhood. Ultrasonography is the diagnostic standard but remains operator-dependent, and no validated machine learning (ML) tools exist for triage or prognostic stratification. We systematically evaluated ML models for diagnosis and prognosis of pediatric intussusception. Methods This PROSPERO-registered systematic review and meta-analysis (CRD420251073590) included studies evaluating ML models for pediatric intussusception diagnosis or prognosis reporting sensitivity, specificity, or AUC. Risk of bias was assessed with PROBAST. A bivariate random-effects model was applied to internally and externally validated datasets, with subgroup analyses by input modality. Results Eleven studies (37 model variants; 36,863 patients) were included. Internally validated ultrasound (US) models (k=4) achieved pooled sensitivity 0.914 (0.829-0.959) and specificity 0.980 (0.939-0.994). Externally validated US models (k=3) showed sensitivity 0.946 (0.909-0.969) and specificity 0.958 (0.918-0.979). Abdominal radiograph (AXR) triage models performed lower externally (sensitivity 0.800 [0.725-0.859]; specificity 0.748 [0.662-0.819]), consistent with a screening role. Notably, AI assistance improved junior readers' specificity by 15.9 percentage points overall (up to 37.6 points for the most junior readers), and AI-assisted junior sonographers cut ultrasound examination time by 61% without loss of diagnostic accuracy. Possible publication bias was detected (Deeks' p=0.021). Prognostic AUCs ranged from 0.555 to 0.962. Conclusions US-based ML models demonstrate high, externally robust diagnostic accuracy. AXR models suit screening but need further validation. No study reported clinical endpoint data. Multicenter prospective validation outside Asia and regulatory pathway development are required before implementation. Until then, AXR-based models should be positioned as an adjunct that raises suspicion, never as a gate that determines which child receives an ultrasound. Level of evidence Level III - Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of retrospective diagnostic accuracy studies.

title: CONGENITAL HEPATOPULMONARY FUSION IN RIGHT CONGENITAL DIAPHRAGMATIC HERNIA: SURGICAL STRATEGY AND OUTCOMES IN A MULTICENTER COHORT.
abstract: Aim Congenital hepatopulmonary fusion (CHPF) is a rare anomaly associated with right congenital diaphragmatic hernia (RCDH), for which optimal diagnosis and surgical management remain undefined. This study aimed to explore the impact of surgical separation on outcomes. Methods A retrospective multicenter study reviewed neonates with intraoperatively or radiologically confirmed CHPF associated with RCDH. Demographic data, imaging, surgical strategy, and outcomes were analyzed. Patients were stratified according to whether surgical separation of the fusion was performed (CHPF-S) or not (CHPF-NS). Results Forty-three patients were included (26 CHPF-S and 17 CHPF-NS). Prenatal diagnosis of RCDH occurred in 20.9% of cases, while most diagnoses were made postnatally. Imaging findings suggestive of CHPF were identified preoperatively in a minority of patients, with computed tomography angiography providing additional information regarding vascular anatomy in selected cases. Baseline demographic characteristics, gestational age, birth weight, and CDH defect distribution were comparable between groups. The age at surgical repair differed, however not significantly, with earlier intervention in the CHPF-S group (9.0 ± 15.8 vs 17.9 ± 24.2 days, p=0.099). Complete parenchymal fusion was more frequently observed in the CHPF-NS group, whereas partial fusion was more common in the CHPF-S group. Pulmonary hypertension occurred in 55.8% of patients and extracorporeal life support was required in 7.0%. Overall mortality was 27.9%, including 7 deaths in the CHPF-NS group and 5 in the CHPF-S group (41.2% vs 19.2%, p=0.117), predominantly related to severe pulmonary hypertension. Conclusions Surgical separation of the fusion may be selectively advisable in hemodynamically stable patients with a thin membrane or partial fusion, although non-separation often remains prudent. In critically ill neonates, patch repair or closure around the fused organs without separation represents a safer alternative. Early suspicion of CHPF in RCDH and thorough preoperative planning are essential to optimize outcomes.

title: Utilizing light energy transformation in nanostructures for targeted diagnostic and therapeutic applications.
abstract: Theranostics, a combination of therapy and diagnostics, represents a paradigm change in precision medicine with the ability to monitor diseases in real time and deliver targeted treatment. Nanomaterials are state-of-the-art technology for photo-energy conversion-based therapeutic action and diagnostic imaging; note the remarkable temporal and spatial precision that uses light as a driving force. This review highlights recent advances in the design and application of such nanomaterials for converting light into demand responses via mechanisms including photoluminescence (PL), photothermal conversion for photothermal therapy (PTT), photoacoustic imaging (PAI), photoelectric effect, SERS-based detection, and photodynamic therapy (PDT). Such light-activated systems are versatile platforms for the treatment of various diseases like arthritis, cancer, neurodegenerative disorders, and retinal degeneration. By integrating multiple therapeutic and diagnostic modalities into a single nanoscale system, photoactive nanomaterials hold the potential to achieve enhanced treatment efficacy with minimal side effects. However, rapid advances are still hindered by challenges related to maximizing tissue penetration and biocompatibility, as well as activation in physiological settings. Nevertheless, the synergy of light-based science and nanotechnology is enabling next-generation precision theranostics and dynamic tools for personalized medicine for physicians. For these intelligent nanoplatforms to reach their full potential in practical healthcare applications, more interdisciplinary research and clinical translation are required.

title: Sonographic evolution of customized CaHA-CMC:CPM hybrid dermal fillers: a six-month high-frequency ultrasound case series.
abstract: Introduction The Cohesive polydensified matrix (CPM) gels are popular Hyaluronic acid (HA) gels along with the dermal filler calcium hydroxylapatite (CaHA-CMC). In recent years, CaHA-CMC has also been increasingly utilized as a biostimulatory agent due to its capacity to promote tissue regeneration. While each product is safe and effective when injected separately, combining CaHA-CMC and CPM in a customized CaHA-CMC:CPM admixture within the same syringe offers additional advantages including reduced treatment time and fewer injections, as well as complementary mechanisms of action: CPM compensates for the early volume loss associated with resorption of the CaHA-CMC carboxymethyl cellulose carrier, while CaHA-CMC stimulates neocollagenesis. As a noninvasive imaging modality, high-frequency dermatologic ultrasound enables evaluation of both short- and long-term post-procedure filler location and its interaction with surrounding soft tissues. Objective To describe high-frequency ultrasound findings at baseline and immediately after treatment, as well as at 30, 90, and 180 days following injection of a customized CaHA-CMC:CPM admixture. Method This descriptive longitudinal case series employed high-frequency ultrasound (20 MHz) performed at baseline, immediately post-injection, and at 30, 90, and 180 days following treatment with a customized CaHA-CMC:CPM admixture. Various admixture formulations were used, combining CaHA-CMC with CPM fillers of differing densities (20.0, 22.5, 25.5, or 26.0 mg/mL) and rheology from the CPM gel range. Dilution ratios ranged from 1:1 to 1:4, and injections were performed in different facial regions. Results Five patients underwent treatment and safety assessment; two female participants, aged 34 and 70 years, completed all predefined longitudinal ultrasound assessments and were included in the imaging analysis. On ultrasound, CaHA-CMC appeared as hyperechoic deposits with variable posterior acoustic shadowing. Variations in sonographic appearance were observed across the evaluated admixtures, anatomical regions, and follow-up timepoints. In general, a progressive reduction in sonographic distinction between the injected material and surrounding tissues was observed over time across the treated areas. Conclusion High-frequency ultrasound enabled longitudinal visualization of the injection technique, precise anatomical layer of hybrid filler placement, changes in sonographic distinction from the surrounding tissues over time, and variability in echogenicity related to product concentration and density. Exploratory three-dimensional imaging provided complementary information regarding regional volumetric changes and directional surface displacement; however, these findings should be interpreted descriptively and require confirmation in larger studies.

title: Axillo-lateral advancement flap for upper inner quadrant and upper central breast defects: A single-centre case series demonstrating early outcomes.
abstract: Background Reconstruction of upper inner quadrant following BCS remains technically challenging due to limited local tissue availability, thin pre-sternal soft tissue, and high aesthetic visibility. We describe our experience with the axillo-lateral advancement flap (ALAF) for reconstruction of the upper inner quadrant and upper centrally located breast defects, emphasizing on technical feasibility and early outcomes. Methodology This single-centre case series included 27 patients undergoing BCS with immediate reconstruction using ALAF between August 2024 and July 2025. Patients with tumours having a size ≤5 cm, located in the UIQ or upper central area of breast, who are undergoing breast conservation surgery either upfront or post neoadjuvant chemotherapy, were included. The primary endpoint was to assess early aesthetic outcomes using a 5-point likert scale following completion of adjuvant radiotherapy. Secondary outcomes included postoperative complications, margin status, margin re-excision rates and adequacy of axillary surgery. Results Median age of the study population was 57 years and median tumour size was 26 mm. Nineteen tumours were located in the UIQ and the rest in the upper central quadrant between 11 and 1 o clock. Intraoperative margin revision was required in 14.8% of cases, with no re-excisions following final histopathology. The mean closest margin was 4.03 mm. Among patients undergoing ALND, the median lymph node yield was 17.5. Postoperative complications included seroma (7.4%), wound infection (3.7%), and partial flap necrosis (3.7%). Median aesthetic scores across all domains were 4 (range 2-5). Median follow-up was 7.2 months (range: 6.1-11.5 months). Conclusions ALAF appears to be a feasible reconstructive option for selected upper inner quadrant and upper central area breast defects, demonstrating encouraging early aesthetic outcomes. However, given the non-comparative design, small sample size, limited follow-up, and use of a non-validated aesthetic assessment tool, further prospective studies with standardized outcome measures are required to establish its oncologic safety and comparative effectiveness.
