Materials and methods: A two-stage self-supervised DL-framework was trained separately for pelvic and brain MRI utilizing three public datasets. The first stage compressed normal image data into discrete representations, and a second stage modeled the representation distribution. Anomaly-evidence was obtained by combining perceptual image differences with token-surprisal scores via negative log-likelihood estimation. Automated detection was evaluated for two anatomical cohorts: pelvis, encompassing both synthetic global anomalies and real clinical anomalies, and brain, comprising clinically annotated anomalies. Performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). For each cohort, a subset of normal images was reserved for analysis. Results: Promising exploratory performance across evaluation cohorts was obtained. AUCs were 0.97 (95% CI 0.96-0.99) for synthetic pelvic anomalies, 0.95 (95% CI 0.90-1.00) for clinical pelvic anomalies, and 0.81 (95% CI 0.74-0.87) for brain anomalies. Qualitative heatmap analysis showed spatial agreement between detected anomalies and reference annotations. Conclusions: The framework variations showed promising anomaly detection performance across pelvic and brain MRI, supporting its potential for automated MRI quality control in radiotherapy. Heatmap-based visualization further improved interpretability by spatially localizing detected anomalies.

title: Aromatherapy for Anxiety and Pain in Radiologic and Interventional Procedures a Scoping Review.
abstract: Objective To describe the scope of evidence on the use and effects of aromatherapy for reducing anxiety and pain in adults undergoing radiologic and interventional procedures. Design Scoping review guided by the Arksey and O'Malley framework and reported using PRISMA‑ScR guidelines. Data sources A comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Library was conducted for studies published between 2013 and 2025. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cohort studies, case series, or pilot studies involving adults receiving an aromatherapy intervention during a diagnostic or interventional radiology procedure, with anxiety and/or pain as outcomes. Twenty-six RCTs met inclusion criteria. Data extraction captured essential oil (EO) type, delivery method, exposure duration, outcome measures, and main findings. Results Lavender was the most frequently studied EO, followed by peppermint, rose-based oils, citrus oils, chamomile, clary sage, Osmanthus fragrans, and Cananga odorata. EO's were delivered using cotton balls, gauze, aromatherapy tabs, patches, masks, inhalers, and diffusers. Anxiety was more frequently evaluated than pain. Reductions in anxiety were commonly reported, particularly in studies using lavender-based interventions, while findings related to pain were more variable. Marked heterogeneity in EO composition, delivery approaches, procedures, and outcome measurement tools limit cross-study comparison and generalizability. Conclusions Aromatherapy, particularly lavender, may reduce procedural anxiety, while evidence supporting pain reduction remains limited. Substantial methodological variability highlights the need for standardized protocols, transparent reporting of EO composition, and rigorous study designs to clarify clinical utility. Nursing practice implications Consistent with the American Society for Pain Management Nursing's emphasis on integrative, evidence-based care, aromatherapy may serve as a safe, nonpharmacologic adjunct to support patient well-being, particularly for procedural anxiety. Safe implementation requires nursing competency in EO selection, delivery methods, contraindications, and patient screening. Continued nursing leadership and advocacy are essential to advance multimodal, patient-centered approaches to procedural pain and anxiety management across care settings.

title: Re-irradiation for recurrent high-grade glioma: current evidence and practical considerations.
abstract: Re-irradiation is an increasingly important salvage option for patients with recurrent high-grade glioma and glioblastoma, but its use is complicated by limited prospective evidence, heterogeneous treatment approaches, and concern for cumulative toxicity to the brain and critical neurologic structures. Available studies suggest that carefully selected patients may achieve meaningful local control, symptom relief, and preservation of neurologic function, although a consistent overall survival benefit has not been demonstrated. Treatment decisions therefore require individualized assessment of performance status, neurologic function, disease volume and pattern, interval from prior radiation therapy, expected prognosis, alternative salvage options, and overlap with previously irradiated organs at risk. In this expert opinion, we summarize the contemporary evidence supporting brain re-irradiation and discuss available techniques; we also describe a practical, organ-at-risk-driven framework for patient selection, target delineation, fractionation, cumulative dose assessment, and integration of systemic therapy. Re-irradiation can be delivered safely in selected patients, but treatment intensity should remain closely aligned with anatomy, prognosis, therapeutic alternatives, and patient goals.

title: Multicenter Evaluation of a Deep Learning Model for Automatic Contouring of Cardiac Substructures in Adults.
abstract: Purpose Efficient delineation of cardiac substructures is essential for assessing radiation-induced cardiac toxicity in thoracic radiotherapy. We clinically evaluated a deep learning model designed for automated segmentation of these structures. Methods and materials The model built in collaboration with XXX (XXX) generated 21 cardiac substructures (whole heart, chambers, coronary arteries, valves, and great vessels). Five radiation oncologists rated raw contours on thirty contrast-enhanced CTs from two institutions using a 4-point Likert scale (3 = no correction, 2 = minor/moderate correction, 1 = major correction, 0 = not performed) and applied corrections when needed. Dice Similarity Coefficients (DSC) and 95th-percentile Hausdorff distances (HD95) were computed to compare model versus reference contours, clinician-corrected versus reference contours, and model versus STAPLE contours. Results Of 630 structures, 93.8% were scored either 3 or ≥2, and 6.2% received 1 by at least one clinician. For the coronary arteries (210 structures), 88.5% were scored either 3 or ≥ 2. Contour generation took approximately 1 min, with a median review and correction time of 7.0 min per CT (IQR, 5.8-9.8). The median DSC between the model and reference contours was 1.0 across all structures, while it ranged from 0.92 to 1.0 for clinician-corrected versus reference contours. Overall, HD95 was below 5 mm, for both clinicians versus reference and model versus STAPLE. Conclusions The deep learning model provided satisfactory segmentation of cardiac substructures on contrast-enhanced CT, including coronary arteries. Its integration into a widely adopted treatment planning system lays the foundation for broad clinical implementation.

title: Two-Year Outcomes of the XXX Trial: Longitudinal Analysis of Safety, PSA Kinetics, and Patient-Reported Outcomes.
abstract: Purpose To assess the 2-year incidence and longitudinal trajectory of grade (G) ≥2 genitourinary (GU) and gastrointestinal (GI) adverse events (AEs) following single-dose ablative radiotherapy (SDRT) for organ-confined prostate cancer (PCa), alongside associated changes in patient-reported outcomes (PROs) and PSA kinetics. Methods XXX (XXX) is a single-institution prospective study enrolling patients with unfavorable intermediate-risk or selected high-risk organ-confined PCa treated with SDRT delivering 24 Gy in one fraction to the prostate and seminal vesicles. Treatment incorporated urethra-sparing and intrafraction motion control and was delivered on a linear accelerator using a 10-MV flattening filter-free single partial arc in combination with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT). AEs were graded using CTCAE v5.0. PSA and testosterone were monitored longitudinally, and scheduled multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) were performed to assess radiological response. PROs were assessed using EORTC QLQ-C30, QLQ-PR25, IPSS, and IIEF questionnaires. Mixed-effects models evaluated longitudinal trajectories and associations with baseline and dosimetric factors. Results Thirty patients were treated. At 2 years, no ≥G3 AEs were observed. Cumulative G2 GU and GI AEs were 23% and 7%, respectively. Two years point prevalent G2 GU and GI AEs were 10% and 3%, respectively. Longitudinal analysis showed an overall stable safety profile, with higher baseline IPSS and bladder trigone D1cc significantly associated with higher GU AEs. PRO analyses demonstrated statistically significant changes in urinary domains, although effect sizes remained below minimal important difference thresholds, indicating no clinically meaningful deterioration. Baseline symptom burden strongly predicted long-term PROs trajectories. Biochemical relapse-free survival was 100% at 2 years, with a consistent and significant PSA decline over time and local radiological control confirmed by mpMRI. Testosterone recovery occurred in 76% of patients receiving ADT. Conclusions Single-fraction 24 Gy SDRT combined with ADT was feasible and well tolerated, with low rates of ≥G2 AEs and largely maintained quality of life at 2 years in patients with unfavorable localized prostate cancer. Early oncologic outcomes are encouraging but require confirmation with longer follow-up and comparative validation.

title: Streamlining Liver SABR: Validation and Initial Experience of Bulk Density Override Based Single-Session, Simulation-Free Adaptive Workflow.
abstract: Purpose Conventional liver stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) typically requires a CT simulation visit followed by multiple treatment fractions, which can increase patient burden and limit access. We propose an approach that consolidates imaging, planning, adaptation, and delivery into one session, utilizing an MR-guided adaptive workflow. We report here the workflow and dosimetric validation of a streamlined bulk density override (BDO) strategy and the initial clinical implementation of this simulation-free approach. Methods and materials A single-institution phase II trial was designed to deliver liver SABR (30-40 Gy in 1 fraction) in a single-session using an MR-guided Linac for patients with liver cancers using BDO strategy. To validate dosimetric accuracy, 17 previously treated single-fraction liver SABR plans were recalculated retrospectively using (1) CT-based electron density and (2) BDO-based density. DVH endpoints and 3D gamma analysis (1%/1mm) were compared. Early clinical experience from the first five trial patients is reported, including dose comparisons between BDO-based calculations and diagnostic CT-based calculations. Results For the retrospective analysis, BDO-based calculation closely matched the CT-based calculation. For the PTV and GTV, the median percent differences were close to zero for all evaluated metrics and the maximum percent differences were all within 2%. For organ-at-risk (OAR) endpoints (chest wall, bowel, liver minus GTV, spinal cord), mean and maximum dose differences were within 0.1 Gy and 0.6 Gy, respectively. The average 3D gamma pass rate was 99.2%. For the first 5 patients treated on trial, BDO- and diagnostic CT-based reference plan metrics agreed within 1.5% for PTV coverage and within 0.5 Gy for key OAR endpoints. The mean gamma pass rate was 98.8%. Conclusions The BDO strategy provides dosimetric agreement comparable to CT-based calculation and supports an efficient and patient-centric single-visit delivery model. Our results support further investigation of simulation-free, single-session MR-guided adaptive liver SABR.

title: Practical considerations of gadoxetate disodium contrast in MRI-guided liver SBRT for primary and secondary liver tumors: optimizing image quality and patient throughput.
abstract: Purpose/objectives Optimal implementation of gadoxetate disodium injection (GDI) in liver-directed MR-guided online adaptive radiotherapy (MRgART) remains poorly characterized. Herein, we evaluated the impact of GDI on physician-reported imaging metrics and quantitative contouring variability during liver MRgART planning. Materials/methods Patients were scanned using a 0.35T MRI onboard the MR-guided LINAC. Pre- and post-contrast TRUFI images were captured at multiple timepoints up to 30 minutes (5-10-minute intervals) following GDI. Four radiation oncologists independently scored each tumor on a 5-point scale (1: poor; 5: excellent) evaluating imaging metrics, such as tumor visualization, border delineation, and image degradation from artifacts. Responses were stratified into pre-contrast, "early" post-contrast (1-15 minutes), and "late" post-contrast (20-30 minutes). Physicians then contoured gross tumor volume (GTV) for 6 patients with either optimal or non-optimal image characteristics. Inter- and intra-observer variability was assessed using Sørensen-Dice coefficient (DICE), Hausdorff distance (HD), volume of tumor not treated (VTNT), and volume of healthy liver erroneously treated (VHL). Comparisons were performed using Mann-Whitney U-test or Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test, as applicable. Results Twenty-three patients with 37 total liver tumors were treated using MRgART (median 50 Gy; 3-5 fractions). Late post-contrast imaging significantly improved tumor visualization (4.45) compared to early post-contrast (3.73; p<0.001) and pre-contrast (3.25; p<0.001). Late post-contrast also significantly improved border delineation (4.38) versus early post-contrast (3.58; p<0.001) and pre-contrast (3.06; p<0.001). In 6 patients selected for contouring analysis, DICE increased from 0.75 to 0.92 (p<0.01) and HD90 decreased from 4.18 mm to 2.00 mm (p<0.01) when GDI was helpful (n=3). Across all 6 patients, median VTNT significantly decreased from 3.68 cm 3 to 0.68 cm 3 (p<0.001). Conclusions GDI administration 20-30 minutes prior to MRgART planning significantly enhances both physician-reported image quality and quantitative contouring accuracy. Its use should be considered in MRgART workflows to minimize potential geographic miss and optimize treatment delivery.

title: Anxiety sensitivity, psychological vulnerability, and brain volumes in borderline personality disorder.
abstract: Aim This study compared AS, psychological vulnerability, and brain volumes in BPD and healthy controls and examined clinical-volumetric associations within BPD. Method Twenty-seven patients with BPD and 28 healthy controls completed the Anxiety Sensitivity Index-3 and the Psychological Vulnerability Scale. Three-dimensional T1-weighted images were acquired using a 1.5-Tesla MRI scanner, and regional volumes were calculated. Results In raw analyses, the BPD group had higher psychological vulnerability and total, cognitive, and social AS scores. After covariate adjustment, only social AS remained significant (p = 0.035). Bilateral putamen, anterior insula, caudate, nucleus accumbens, and total gray matter volumes were larger in the BPD group, persisting after adjustment (all p ≤ 0.018). Differences in left amygdala, posterior and total insula, posterior cingulate gyrus, and white matter volumes lost significance after adjustment. In the BPD group, posterior insula volumes were negatively correlated with total and social AS scores, remaining significant after controlling for confounders (r=-0.471 to -0.611; p = 0.004-0.036). Psychological vulnerability and cognitive AS were not associated with regional volumes. Conclusion Social AS may represent a specific dimension of BPD. Group-level differences in anterior insula and striatal volumes, together with dimensional associations between posterior insula volumes and AS, suggest distinct roles for insular subregions in BPD-related clinical and structural processes.

title: Nasopharyngeal diffuse large b-cell lymphoma in a teenage presenting with cavernous sinus syndrome: A case report.
abstract: Primary lymphoma of the nasopharynx is uncommon and is more commonly seen as an association with other primary pathologies. Nasopharyngeal lymphoma is an aggressive tumor and can affect all age groups but is more commonly seen in middle-aged and older individuals. Majority of these tumors belong to the non-Hodgkin's group. Cavernous sinus syndrome (CSS) is a rare but severe complication indicating advanced aggressive stage of disease with direct extension of tumor into the cavernous sinus. Our patient is a young teenage 18-years old presented to emergency department with the symptoms of left jaw pain (4 months), facial swelling (1 month), bilateral nasal obstruction, dysphagia (1 month), visual loss in left eye and proptosis (1 week) along with weight loss. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) face and neck with contrast performed immediately revealed a nasopharyngeal mass with extension of disease into the left cavernous sinus encasing cavernous part of the left internal carotid artery (ICA), involvement of the left orbital apex, optic chiasm and pituitary gland. Histopathology later confirmed diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL). Laboratory investigations were unremarkable except for an elevated ESR. The patient underwent multidisciplinary management with combined chemotherapy and radiotherapy, demonstrating an excellent response on follow-up MRI and PET-CT, and was discharged with appropriate follow-up instructions. This case highlights early recognition with MRI and histopathological confirmation enables timely chemotherapy, improving outcomes and reducing the risk of permanent neurological sequelae.

title: Delayed radiographic diagnosis of distal femoral metastases in breast cancer: A case report from Cocody University Teaching Hospital (Côte d'ivoire).
abstract: Bone metastases represent a frequent complication of breast cancer, affecting more than one third of patients. Delayed investigation of persistent focal bone pain in a breast cancer patient can lead to serious consequences. We report a case of delayed radiographic diagnosis of distal femur metastases in a breast cancer patient, where the initial standard X-ray was normal. The diagnosis of bone metastasis was established by a second X-ray 11 months later, following disease progression. This case highlights the limitations of conventional radiography and highlights the importance of using PET-CT, MRI, or bone scintigraphy imaging modalities methods for early detection of metastatic lesions to guide therapeutic management.

title: The 'Upstairs-Downstairs' heart with complete main pulmonary artery agenesis and PDA-dependent pulmonary circulation: A rare structural intersection characterized by multi detector computed tomography.
abstract: Superior-inferior ventricular arrangement is an exceedingly rare form of congenital cardiac malposition, representing fewer than 0.1% of all congenital heart diseases, and is almost invariably associated with complex intracardiac anomalies. We report a 3-year-old male who presented with persistent cyanosis, exertional dyspnea, and failure to thrive. Prospective ECG-gated CT angiography demonstrated situs solitus with levocardia. A superior-inferior ventricular arrangement was present, with the morphologic left ventricle positioned superior to the morphologic right ventricle. The great arteries were normally related, with a left-sided aortic arch. A large ventricular septal defect was identified. Pulmonary atresia was present, characterized by the absence of the right ventricular outflow tract, pulmonary valve, and main pulmonary artery. Native confluent branch pulmonary arteries were present and received pulmonary blood flow through a large patent ductus arteriosus supplying the left pulmonary artery, with additional small systemic-to-pulmonary collateral vessels. The morphologic right ventricle was dilated and hypertrophied, with associated enlargement of the right atrium. Pulmonary venous drainage was normal, and no abnormalities of the systemic venous drainage were identified. This case underscores the critical role of cardiac CT angiography in comprehensive anatomical delineation of rare and complex congenital cardiac malformations, with direct implications for surgical planning and prognostication.

title: One-stop photon-counting CT angiography for simultaneous assessment of cardio-cerebrovascular lesions: A case report.
abstract: We report a 73-year-old male admitted for 2-year progressive dysuria, with incidental detection of abnormal cardiovascular signs on physical examination. Initial evaluation via energy-integrating detector computed tomography (EID-CT) coronary angiography and cranial magnetic resonance imaging identified key vascular abnormalities, while subsequent photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT) combined cardio-cerebral computed tomography angiography (CTA) provided more detailed assessment of stenosis severity, plaque composition, and the entire vascular bed. The combined PCD-CT scan delineated synchronous lesions in detail: proximal left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery plaque, ascending aortic dilatation with left coronary sinus aneurysm compressing the left atrium, and occlusion of the intracranial right vertebral artery. Importantly, PCD-CT cardio-cerebral CTA yielded a lower radiation dose compared with standalone EID-CT coronary angiography. With spectral reconstruction, the severity of LAD stenosis was re-evaluated and interpreted as mild stenosis, a lower grade than that assessed by EID-CT; meanwhile, 0.4 mm thin-slice imaging enabled detailed compositional analysis of the coronary plaque, with imaging features suggestive of a stable plaque. Based on multidisciplinary discussion integrating all imaging findings and clinical context, a treatment strategy was formulated: prioritize high-risk aortic lesion management, synchronously perform coronary artery bypass grafting for myocardial ischemia prevention, and electively address intracranial stenosis. This case demonstrates the preliminary clinical value of PCD-CT as a supportive imaging modality for the evaluation and multidisciplinary management of concurrent cardio-cerebrovascular diseases.

title: Infective endocarditis presenting as febrile stroke and complicated with multi-territorial systemic embolization in a young woman: A case report.
abstract: Infective endocarditis (IE) is a life-threatening condition frequently complicated by systemic embolization, most commonly involving the central nervous system, spleen, and kidneys. In a young patient, a febrile ischemic stroke should be considered infective endocarditis until proven otherwise, given the diagnostic and prognostic stakes of an early diagnosis. Multi-territorial embolic dissemination at presentation, however, remains uncommon and carries substantial clinical implications. We report the case of a 49-year-old woman with an undocumented mitral valve disease who presented with acute left hemiparesis and a one-month history of high-grade fever. Brain MRI revealed an acute ischemic stroke of the right middle cerebral artery territory. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated mobile vegetations on the mitral valve, and blood cultures isolated Streptococcus species, establishing a definite diagnosis of infective endocarditis. Contrast-enhanced CT of the brain, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, together with spinal MRI, revealed extensive systemic embolization involving five distinct vascular territories: a cerebral septic embolic focus, splenic and renal infarction, a mycotic aneurysm of the ileocolic artery, and infectious spondylodiscitis. This case underscores that a febrile ischemic stroke in a young patient warrants urgent screening for infective endocarditis, and highlights the value of a systematic, whole-body imaging work-up in detecting clinically silent embolic complications and guiding patient management.

title: Isolated cerebellopontine angle metastasis from breast cancer: The added value of MR spectroscopy.
abstract: Cerebellopontine angle (CPA) tumors are predominantly vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas; metastatic lesions in this location are rare, particularly in the absence of multiple brain metastases. We report the case of a 53-year-old woman with a history of invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast in HER2-positive metastatic relapse, in whom brain MRI revealed a single 28 × 24 mm mass in the right cerebellopontine angle. The lesion was isointense on T1- and T2-weighted images, contained fluid components, and showed restricted diffusion (ADC 0.64 × 10⁻³ mm²/s) with intense peripheral enhancement after gadolinium administration. MR spectroscopy demonstrated markedly elevated Cho/NAA (6.73) and Cho/Cr (5.72) ratios within the lesion, with a normal perilesional spectroscopic profile, favoring a secondary lesion and allowing the main differential diagnoses to be excluded without biopsy. The patient underwent stereotactic radiotherapy (30 Gy in 5 fractions), with significant regression of the lesion on follow-up MRI at five months. This case illustrates the role of MR spectroscopy in the non-invasive characterization of atypical cerebellopontine angle lesions.

title: Recurrent papillary thyroid carcinoma with brachiocephalic vein tumor thrombus: A rare case report.
abstract: Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) generally has an excellent prognosis and an indolent clinical course. However, major vascular invasion with tumor thrombus formation is exceedingly rare. We report the case of a 63-year-old woman with recurrent PTC presenting five years after total thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine therapy. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated recurrent disease within the thyroidectomy bed, extensive cervical nodal metastases, retrosternal extension, pulmonary nodules, and tumor thrombus involving the left brachiocephalic vein near the SVC junction. The patient underwent extensive surgical management, including left modified neck dissection, median sternotomy, en bloc resection of recurrent disease, thrombectomy, and primary repair of the brachiocephalic vein. Histopathological examination confirmed recurrent papillary thyroid carcinoma with vascular tumor thrombosis. Postoperatively, the patient received adjuvant radioactive iodine therapy. At 12-month follow-up, serum thyroglobulin levels were undetectable, and imaging studies demonstrated no evidence of locoregional recurrence. This case highlights a rare and aggressive presentation of recurrent PTC with major venous involvement and demonstrates that satisfactory short-term disease control can be achieved through aggressive multidisciplinary management.

title: Lenticulostriate vasculopathy in neonates: An imaging marker with heterogeneous clinical significance.
abstract: Lenticulostriate vasculopathy (LSV) is a relatively common cranial ultrasound finding in neonates, characterized by linear or branching hyperechogenic striations within the basal ganglia and/or thalamus along the lenticulostriate arteries. Although initially associated with congenital infections, particularly cytomegalovirus (CMV), LSV is now recognized in a broad range of clinical settings, and its prognostic significance remains controversial. We report 3 neonatal cases illustrating the heterogeneous contexts in which LSV may occur. The first case was a term male neonate with transient respiratory distress and normal neurological examination; cranial ultrasound on day 3 showed unilateral right-sided fine linear striations in the basal ganglia without parenchymal abnormalities. Infectious workup was negative and outcome was favorable. The second case involved a 36-week male neonate born after acute fetal distress, with severe respiratory distress requiring resuscitation. Cranial ultrasound demonstrated unilateral left-sided LSV without hemorrhagic or hypoxic-ischemic lesions; subsequent brain MRI was normal, with favorable follow-up and slight regression of the ultrasound abnormalities. The third case was a term female neonate with prolonged jaundice, hypotonia, hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, and abnormal liver function tests. Cranial ultrasound revealed bilateral branching striations, and congenital CMV infection was confirmed by urine PCR. These cases highlight the nonspecific nature of LSV, which may occur as an isolated finding, with perinatal hypoxic or hemodynamic disturbances, or with congenital infection. Recognition of LSV should be interpreted in the clinical context, with targeted investigation when abnormalities are present, while isolated forms may have a favorable outcome.

title: Stopping too soon: Search termination and subsequent search misses in diagnostic radiography.
abstract: Introduction Diagnostic radiography requires balancing image evaluation, dose optimisation, and workflow efficiency within time-constrained clinical environments. Image acceptance depends on detecting technical issues and determining when further inspection is unnecessary and when an image is sufficient for clinical purposes. Visual search theory suggests that observers rely on internal stopping rules to guide termination decisions, yet their role in radiographic image adequacy remains underexplored. This paper develops a model of radiographic search termination. Methods A conceptual model was developed through narrative synthesis of literature from cognitive psychology, medical image perception and radiology. Relevant studies were selected to identify key constructs, including quitting rules, subsequent search misses, inattentional blindness and confidence during incomplete search. These constructs were integrated to generate a radiography-specific framework explaining search termination. Results A model is presented in which radiographic image evaluation is considered a multiple-target visual search task governed by an internal stopping threshold. This threshold reflects when the expected benefit of continued inspection falls below its perceived cost. It may be shaped by perceptual evidence, time pressure, workload, interruptions, target prevalence, patient presentation, observer confidence, experience and departmental norms. The model proposes three candidate termination patterns: global-impression termination, target-substitution termination and constraint-driven termination. It also identifies structured second-pass inspection, confidence calibration and feedback on missed secondary inadequacies as theoretically informed strategies requiring empirical investigation. Conclusion Framing image acceptance as a stopping-policy decision provides a cognitive explanation for variability in adequacy assessment and repeat imaging. Search termination reflects a dynamic balance between thoroughness and efficiency under uncertainty. Implications for practice Integrating visual search theory into education and workflow design may support better calibration of stopping thresholds, improving image quality, reducing unnecessary repeats, and supporting clinically meaningful decision-making.

title: Diagnosing endometriosis in adolescents using ultrasound and MRI: A scoping review of imaging approach and implementation considerations.
abstract: Introduction Imaging is increasingly used for adult endometriosis, but evidence supporting adolescent imaging approaches remains unclear. This scoping review mapped evidence on imaging-based diagnosis of endometriosis in adolescents and young people, including ultrasound and MRI approaches, imaging-detected disease phenotypes, consent, acceptability, and AI-assisted imaging. Methods Studies involving people with suspected or confirmed endometriosis were eligible if participants were aged 14-25 years or the population was explicitly described as adolescent, teenage, youth, or young adult. Author-defined adolescent cohorts could therefore include participants younger than 14 years. MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, CINAHL and Web of Science were searched, alongside grey literature and reference lists. Screening and extraction were completed independently in duplicate. Data were synthesised descriptively. Results Thirty-five evidence sources were included: nine primary studies and 26 secondary sources. The primary evidence base was limited, heterogeneous and mostly specialist-based. Ultrasound was the sole or initial modality in eight of nine primary studies; MRI was used in four. Imaging findings were most consistent for ovarian endometrioma and posterior deep endometriosis. Superficial disease was poorly captured, and normal imaging remained common in symptomatic cohorts. Secondary sources commonly described ultrasound-first approaches, with selective use of transvaginal ultrasound, transrectal ultrasound, or MRI. Acceptability, feasibility, consent and refusal were frequently discussed in secondary sources but rarely measured in primary studies. No adolescent-specific primary studies evaluated AI-assisted imaging. Conclusion Imaging is recommended in clinical guidance for adolescent endometriosis and evaluated in selected cohorts, but the evidence remains limited, heterogeneous and largely adult-derived. Implications for practice Imaging is an important component of adolescent endometriosis assessment. Modality choice and examination approach should be individualised through informed consent. Negative imaging should not be interpreted as excluding endometriosis, particularly superficial disease, when symptoms persist.

title: Doses in planning computed tomography in one radiotherapy department: Description of exposure parameters and estimation of organ doses, effective doses and typical doses.
abstract: Introduction Computed tomography (CT) used in radiotherapy (RT) planning involves complex acquisitions protocols, making it essential to evaluate doses and ensure patients' radiological safety. This study aims to evaluate organ doses based on RT planning CT scans, Effective Doses (ED), and Typical Doses, in a Portuguese RT department. Methods The sample included 151 patients who underwent planning CT using the General Electric (GE) Discovery ™ RT scanner. Dosimetric estimates were obtained with the National Cancer Institute Dosimetry System for Computed Tomography (NCICT). For each examination, acquisition parameters, patient anatomical diameters, Volume Computed Tomography Dose Index (CTDI vol ), Dose-Length Product (DLP), organ absorbed doses, and ED were analysed. Results Typical Dose values were proposed, based on the 50th percentile of CTDI vol and DLP distributions of the main RT protocols: head and neck (H&N), central nervous system (CNS), breast, breast and axilla, breast deep inspiration breath hold (DIBH), 4D lung, stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) lung and prostate. Results were compared with the literature, to assess practice and identify optimization areas. Conclusion These findings improve understanding of local practices and highlight the importance of periodic protocol evaluation. Furthermore, this study provides a basis for dose optimization strategies and supports the definition of diagnostic reference levels (DRL) in RT services. Implication for practice This study demonstrates the importance of evaluating and monitoring CT protocols in RT planning to ensure patient safety and minimize radiation exposure. The analysis of organ doses, ED, and local DRL provides concrete values reflecting current practice. These findings can guide protocol adjustments, support definition of typical dose levels and contribute to future optimisation strategies in RT.

title: Impact of multisequence MRI on deep learning-based dose prediction for glioblastoma radiotherapy: A comparative evaluation of CT-only and CT+MRI models.
abstract: Introduction Deep learning-based dose prediction has emerged as a promising approach for supporting automated radiotherapy planning workflows by estimating three-dimensional dose distributions from patient imaging. Although planning CT remains the standard imaging modality, multisequence MRI provides anatomical and tissue-characterization information that may improve prediction accuracy in glioblastoma (GBM) radiotherapy. This study investigated the incremental value of multisequence MRI by comparing CT-only and CT + MRI models using an identical framework. Methods A retrospective cohort of 140 patients with GBM treated with conventionally fractionated radiotherapy (60 Gy in 30 fractions) was analyzed. Two 3D Attention U-Net models were developed: CT-only and CT + MRI incorporating T1-weighted gadolinium-enhanced (T1GD), FLAIR, and T2∗ MRI sequences. Patients were divided into training (n = 100), validation (n = 20), and test (n = 20) cohorts. Models were trained for 130 epochs using Adam optimizer with a composite loss function of 70% mean absolute error (MAE) and 30% mean squared error. Results The CT + MRI model achieved lower MAE than CT-only (5.99 ± 1.45 Gy vs. 6.92 ± 1.74 Gy, p = 0.006). D2 error decreased from 3.51 ± 1.61 Gy to 1.53 ± 1.53 Gy. SSIM improved from 0.564 ± 0.102 to 0.599 ± 0.134 (p = 0.017), and PSNR increased from 16.84 ± 2.17 dB to 18.01 ± 1.92 dB (p = 0.009). Pearson correlation coefficients were 0.929 and 0.937 for CT-only and CT + MRI models, respectively. Conclusion Multisequence MRI improved deep learning-based dose prediction for GBM radiotherapy, particularly spatial dose agreement and high-dose region estimation. Further multicentre validation is required. Implications for practice MRI-enhanced dose prediction may support automated planning workflows by improving predicted dose distributions.

title: Visualizing ventriculoperitoneal shunt valve settings with computed tomography, using extended CT scale reconstructions.
abstract: Introduction Ventriculoperitoneal shunts are commonly evaluated using radiographs to confirm valve settings and catheter integrity. Although modern CT provides detailed soft tissue assessment, valve setting readouts have been unreliable due to insufficient spatial resolution and attenuation range. This study investigated whether image reconstructions with extended CT scale (ECTS) can enable reliable identification of valve settings for three common programmable shunt valve types on routine clinical CT examinations. Methods Fifteen routine head CT examinations from 14 patients with programmable shunt valves (five each of Codman Hakim, Medtronic Strata and Miethke proGAV 2.0) were included. For each examination, multiple reconstructions were generated from raw data, including standard bone-kernel images and ECTS-based reconstructions. One representative image from each reconstruction was evaluated by 15 blinded reviewers, who recorded valve setting and confidence. Accuracy was assessed relative to clinically documented reference settings, with ±1 step considered an acceptable deviation. Results All valve settings were correctly identified within ±1 step on ECTS reconstructions across all three valve types. ECTS significantly improved setting readout compared with standard reconstructions. Neither iterative reconstruction nor metal-artifact reduction provided additional benefit. Conclusion ECTS reconstructions with a small FOV, derived from routine clinical CT head examinations, allowed reliable readout of programmable shunt valve settings for Codman Hakim, Medtronic Strata, and proGAV 2.0 valves. These findings represent an important step toward a unified CT-based approach for ventriculoperitoneal shunt evaluation. Implications for practice Head CT is commonly performed in patients with programmable shunts, often to rule out unintended valve settings or dysfunction. Every increased possibility to read the setting directly on CT, such as adding ECTS reconstructions, will directly benefit the patients through increased safety and decreased or waived need for additional projection radiography.

title: Behavioural and environmental strategies implemented by radiographers to care for patients with neurocognitive disorders during medical imaging and therapeutic procedures.
abstract: Introduction As the population ages, radiographers are increasingly likely to care for patients with dementia, Alzheimer's disease and other neurocognitive disorders in medical imaging or radiation therapy departments. Since the cognitive and behavioural presentation of these patients can vary, radiographers must be prepared to adapt their approach. To investigate behavioural and environmental strategies used by radiographers when caring for patients with neurocognitive disorders (NCDs) during medical imaging and radiation therapy procedures. Methods A cross-sectional survey comprising 18 questions was conducted among radiographers working across medical imaging and radiotherapy modalities. The questionnaire explored attitudes towards patients with NCDs, behavioural communication strategies, environmental adaptations, and institutional support measures. Descriptive statistics and thematic analysis of open-ended responses were performed. Results A total of 160 radiographers participated. Most respondents reported positive attitudes toward patients with NCDs, with 94% indicating no fear when interacting with this population. Behavioural communication strategies were frequently used, particularly maintaining eye contact (85%), using simple language (80%), and speaking slowly and clearly (76%). Caregivers were commonly involved to facilitate communication (81%). Despite this, 45% of radiographers reported frustration at not always knowing how to help effectively. Institutional environmental adaptations were limited, with most participants reporting no dementia-specific training (85%) or departmental protocols (78%). Conclusion Radiographers frequently implement behavioural strategies to support patients with NCDs, but this relies on individual initiative rather than structured organisational support, which remains limited. Implications for practice Radiographers should use clear, simple communication strategies with NCD patients, involve caregivers during imaging procedures, and develop dementia-specific training and departmental protocols.

title: Post-registration medical imaging education as a pathway to addressing the specialist deficit in Rwanda: A needs assessment.
abstract: Introduction Sub-Saharan Africa faces a critical shortage of specialist medical imaging practitioners, yet undergraduate training remains insufficient for advanced practice. Rwanda's "4 × 4 Reform" prioritises expanding the radiology workforce, but evidence-based curriculum development for postgraduate education remains lacking. This study aimed to conduct a multi-stakeholder needs assessment to inform the design, structure, and delivery of a proposed Master of Science in Medical Imaging at the University of Rwanda, College of Medicine and Health Sciences. Methods An online cross-sectional survey was conducted nationally, recruiting 210 participants from multiple stakeholder groups, including clinical practitioners, educators, policymakers, and patient representatives. Data were analysed with descriptive statistics and Fisher's exact tests in R. Results Advanced image interpretation skills were identified as hugely lacking by 72.9% of respondents. Diagnostic ultrasound (68.8%), pattern recognition (65.2%), computed tomography (61.7%), and magnetic resonance imaging (60.7%) were the top priorities. Notably, 79.0% (n = 166) of stakeholders expected graduates to develop leadership and management skills, followed by teaching and curriculum development (73.8%). Fisher's exact tests comparing clinical practitioners (n = 142) with other stakeholders (n = 68) found no significant differences across all seven skills assessed (ultrasound: p = 0.2; pattern recognition: p = 0.2; CT: p = 0.4; MRI: p = 0.5; radiography: p > 0.9; nuclear medicine: p = 0.9; radiation therapy: p = 0.6). Conclusions This empirical assessment in Rwanda reveals an urgent need for specialist training that integrates advanced clinical competencies with leadership and education skills. Implications for practice This study offers a guide for integrating advanced clinical skills with leadership and educational competencies into postgraduate curricula, directly addressing critical workforce shortages in low-resource settings.

title: Skill mix redesign in Italian radiation oncology: A technical note on advanced practice radiation therapists.
abstract: Introduction Radiation oncology departments are increasingly required to deliver complex, technology-dependent care while facing medical workforce constraints. In the Italian context, reduced attractiveness of radiation oncology training and increasing workflow complexity highlight the need for transparent skill-mix models. This technical note proposes a practical framework for advanced practice radiation therapists (APRTs) to support selected technical, organisational and protocol-driven components of the radiotherapy pathway while preserving radiation oncologist (RO) accountability for clinical decision-making. Methods A structured narrative and implementation-oriented approach was used. Literature on radiotherapy utilisation, workforce constraints, APRT roles, time-driven activity-based costing and governance was integrated with the Italian professional context. Activities were classified according to medical decision intensity, technical standardisation, patient-specific variability, safety risk and suitability for protocol-based execution. Results Potential APRT roles include simulation preparation, image-guided radiotherapy matching within defined thresholds, organ-at-risk contouring support, auto-contouring review, dosimetric data extraction, toxicity screening, quality assurance, incident reporting and pathway coordination. Non-delegable medical responsibilities include treatment indication, informed consent, prescription, target definition, final plan approval, adaptive decisions affecting prescription or target coverage, toxicity management and oncological follow-up. Safe implementation requires formal education, clinical mentorship, competency assessment, written standard operating procedures, escalation rules, audit and multidisciplinary governance. Conclusion APRTs should not be viewed as substitutes for ROs, but as a structured workforce strategy to preserve medical decision-making capacity and improve workflow resilience in Italian radiotherapy services. Implications for practice Prospective time-motion, safety and health-economic evaluations are needed to quantify the operational impact and transferability of APRT implementation.

title: Humanity in the loop: Reframing artificial intelligence and the global medical imaging divide.
abstract: Objectives Access to radiology and nuclear medicine remains profoundly unequal across global health systems. Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) face persistent shortages in imaging equipment, specialist workforce, digital infrastructure, maintenance, regulation and sustainable financing. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly positioned as a mechanism to improve imaging access, but it may also reinforce existing inequities. This narrative review examines the potential for discriminative, generative and agentic AI to reduce or widen inequities in LMIC medical imaging and proposes a sociotechnical governance framework based on the concept of Humanity-in-the-Loop. Key findings Discriminative AI may improve image interpretation, triage, segmentation, quantification and image-quality assessment; generative AI may enhance reporting, education, translation, communication, synthetic data generation and research workflows; and agentic AI may coordinate referrals, scheduling, follow-up, supply logistics and imaging pathways. They may also exacerbate inequity through data colonialism, algorithmic under-performance, dataset shift, infrastructure dependence, commercial lock-in, second-tier automation, liability transfer and unequal participation in AI research and development. Conclusion Human-in-the-loop governance is insufficient for equitable AI implementation in LMIC medical imaging because the assumptions underpinning effective human oversight are often absent in resource-constrained settings. The proposed Humanity-in-the-Loop sociotechnical framework embeds equity, local agency, contextual validity and public benefit throughout the AI lifecycle. The framework comprises six interconnected domains: patient humanity, workforce humanity, community humanity, data humanity, system humanity and global humanity. Implications for practice Responsible implementation of AI in medical imaging requires governance frameworks that extend beyond algorithm performance to include workforce development, data sovereignty, infrastructure, community priorities, equitable partnerships and sustainable capacity building. Adoption of a Humanity-in-the-Loop approach may help ensure that AI narrows rather than widens the medical imaging divide between high-income countries and LMICs.

title: Enhancing CT anatomy learning in radiotherapy education using Eclipse treatment planning system and IMAIOS e-anatomy: A pilot study.
abstract: Introduction Accurate interpretation of cross-sectional computed tomography (CT) anatomy is fundamental to therapeutic radiography practice, underpinning radiotherapy planning and verification. Emerging evidence suggests that three-dimensional educational technologies may enhance anatomy learning compared with traditional teaching approaches. This pilot study evaluated the impact of using the Varian Eclipse treatment planning system (TPS) as an anatomy learning tool alongside IMAIOS e-Anatomy within radiotherapy education. Methods A quasi-experimental single-group pre-test/post-test study was conducted with first-year students (n = 18) within a university Radiotherapy and Oncology programme. Anatomy teaching using Eclipse TPS and IMAIOS e-Anatomy supplemented the existing curriculum. CT anatomy knowledge was assessed at baseline (T1), five weeks post-intervention (T2), and three months post-intervention (T3) using a 40-item questionnaire. Student perceptions of IMAIOS e-Anatomy were also evaluated using a modified Technology Acceptance Model questionnaire. Results Sixteen students completed all knowledge assessments. Mean knowledge scores increased from 37.03 (SD = 7.32) at T1 to 60.78 (SD = 12.99) at T2 and remained elevated at T3 (58.44, SD = 12.31). Knowledge scores improved significantly over time (F(2,30) = 52.70, p < .001, partial η 2 = 0.778), with significant improvements between T1 and T2 and between T1 and T3 (both p < .001), while the difference between T2 and T3 was not significant (p = .42). Students reported perceived usefulness, confidence, engagement, and intention to continue using IMAIOS e-Anatomy. Conclusion The integration of Eclipse TPS and IMAIOS e-Anatomy was associated with improved CT anatomy knowledge, with gains maintained at three-month follow-up. Students reported high levels of engagement and perceived preparedness for clinical practice. Combining Eclipse TPS and IMAIOS e-Anatomy may support clinically relevant anatomy education in therapeutic radiography. Implications for practice Radiotherapy software and interactive anatomy tools may support learner confidence and preparation for radiotherapy practice, although further evaluation in larger studies is required.

title: CBCT-guided plan-of-the-day adaptive radiotherapy for locally advanced cervical cancer: Feasibility and dosimetric evaluation in a resource-limited setting.
abstract: Introduction Interfractional anatomical variations during pelvic radiotherapy for locally advanced cervical cancer may compromise target coverage and increase organ-at-risk (OAR) irradiation. This study evaluated the feasibility and dosimetric impact of a cone-beam CT (CBCT)-guided Plan-of-the-Day (PoD) adaptive radiotherapy where resources are limited. Methods Twenty patients treated with definitive chemoradiotherapy were prospectively enrolled. Three volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) plans were generated for each patient using planning target volume margins of 7, 10, and 15 mm around the cervical tumour clinical target volume. Daily CBCT imaging was used to select the most appropriate plan according to daily anatomy. The workflow was implemented using standard CBCT-guided IGRT resources without dedicated online adaptive radiotherapy software. Anatomical variations were assessed over 500 treatment fractions, and dose recalculation was performed on 410 fractions. Results Substantial interfractional anatomical variations were observed. Bladder volume was lower than the planning value in 68.2% of fractions, whereas rectal distension exceeded planning values in 74.4%. The reduced-margin plan was selected in 58.8% of fractions, followed by the standard (27%) and large-margin plans (14.2%). Plan selection was significantly associated with bladder and rectal anatomical variations. Target coverage remained satisfactory across all plans (mean PTV V42.75Gy: 96.8-97.5%), with the predefined V95% criterion achieved in 85.7%, 79.8%, and 89.3% of recalculated fractions for the 7-, 10-, and 15 mm plans, respectively. Larger margins significantly increased bladder and rectal V30Gy and V40Gy values. Conclusion A CBCT-guided PoD strategy was feasible using standard IGRT resources and generally maintained high target coverage despite substantial interfractional anatomical variations. Larger margins increased OAR dose-volume parameters, supporting individualized daily plan selection where dedicated online ART infrastructure is unavailable. Implications for practice CBCT-guided PoD offers a strategy where online adaptive radiotherapy is unavailable.

title: Artificial intelligence, disclosure and consent: a comparative review of Australian and European Union legal frameworks for medical imaging.
abstract: To conduct a comparative narrative review of Australian and European approaches to transparency, disclosure, and informed consent in AI-assisted medical imaging, with attention to patient autonomy, professional responsibilities, and regulatory oversight. AI systems are increasingly integrated into medical imaging workflows and offer significant benefits in diagnostic speed, efficiency, and accuracy. However, the reviewed literature highlights substantial concerns relating to transparency, algorithmic bias, automation bias, informed consent, and accountability. Compared with Australia, the European Union has more explicit statutory requirements for transparency, information provided to AI deployers, human oversight, and the governance of high-risk AI systems. Australian regulation remains distributed across privacy law, medical device regulation, common law, state consent legislation, and professional guidance. Current regulatory approaches to AI-assisted medical imaging remain inconsistent internationally. European legislation currently represents a stronger and more comprehensive model for disclosure and transparency obligations compared to Australia's developing framework. Ongoing legal reform, interdisciplinary collaboration, and responsive governance structures will be necessary to address the rapid advancement and increasing integration of AI systems within healthcare. Disclosure should be proportionate to the role, autonomy, risk, and clinical significance of the AI system. Where AI materially affects an examination or diagnostic decision, patients should receive clear information about its involvement, the extent of human oversight, material risks and limitations, how their data may be used, and any reasonably available alternatives. Radiographers and radiologists require appropriate AI literacy and clear local governance to support consistent communication, professional judgement, and accountability.

title: Multi-center comparison of relative stopping power estimation of an ex vivo phantom using clinical X-ray CT scanners and a proton CT prototype.
abstract: Background and purpose Accurate estimation of relative stopping power (RSP) is essential for proton therapy (PT) treatment planning. Emerging X-ray computed tomography (xCT) technologies are enabling more advanced RSP calibration strategies, but may also introduce greater variability across centers. This study aimed to assess inter-center variability in xCT calibration and RSP estimation for proton treatment planning, using a proton CT (pCT) prototype as reference. Material and methods An ex vivo phantom was transported to five European PT centers and one research center, and scanned with both single-energy and dual-energy xCT systems. Acquisitions were performed in three phantom configurations, simulating different anatomical sizes. The reconstructed xCT images were calibrated to RSP according to each center's clinical protocol and compared against the pCT-derived RSP maps. Results Voxel-by-voxel comparison between xCT-based and pCT-based RSP maps showed inter-center RSP variability of about 1% in soft tissues and up to 5% in bone, with larger differences observed for larger phantom sizes. The largest discrepancies (up to 5%) relative to pCT were observed in the same configurations. Centers implementing beam-hardening corrections generally showed closer agreement with pCT, whereas the effect of size-specific HLUTs was tissue- and anatomy-dependent. The impact of these RSP variations on water-equivalent thickness in representative clinical scenarios resulted in a 2σ inter-center variability of 1.09% and 1.39% for brain and prostate cases, respectively. Conclusions This work presents the first inter-center comparison of xCT-based RSP estimation using an ex vivo phantom and pCT measurements as reference. The observed variability highlights the relevance of a comprehensive and standardized validation of xCT calibration protocols.

title: Stereotactic MRI-guided adaptive radiation therapy (SMART) for locally advanced pancreatic cancer: A prospective single-center cohort study.
abstract: Purpose This prospective single-center cohort study evaluated outcomes and toxicity after ablative stereotactic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-guided adaptive radiation therapy (SMART) in patients with locally advanced pancreatic cancer (LAPC). Materials and methods Patients with LAPC treated within the MOMENTUM protocol (NCT04075305) received SMART (50 Gy/5 fractions) on a 1.5 T MRI-linear accelerator. Data were prospectively collected. Overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), risk of local progression, and toxicity were evaluated. Results Between February 2019 and September 2025, 118 patients with LAPC were treated. Median OS from the first SMART fraction was 13.2 months (95 % confidence interval [CI] 10.4-15.9), with a 2-year OS rate of 23.9 % (95 % CI 16.7-34.1). Median OS from diagnosis was 19.6 months (95 % CI 17.8-24.0). Median PFS from the first SMART fraction was 5.6 months (95 % CI 4.3-7.1), and 2-year PFS was 14.8 % (95 % CI 8.8-24.9 %). The cumulative incidence of local progression was 15.0 % at 1 year and 22.2 % at 2 years. Acute grade ≥ III gastrointestinal toxicity occurred in 6/112 assessed patients (5.4 %), including one grade IV ulcer perforation and one grade V duodenal perforation. Late grade ≥ III toxicity occurred in 3/93 assessed patients (3.2 %). Conclusion SMART provided encouraging local control with limited severe toxicity in patients with LAPC, while distant progression remained the dominant pattern of failure.

title: Early target volume dynamics during MR-guided radiotherapy for glioblastoma: first results from the prospective MARGA-I trial.
abstract: Serial MRI during radiotherapy may enable early response assessment and guide adaptive treatment strategies; however, data on intratreatment volumetric changes remain limited. We herein report results of the MARGA-I-study, investigating target volume changes during MR-linac-based radio-(chemo-)therapy. In this prospective single-center-study, 25 patients with glioblastoma were treated on a 0.35-T-MR-linac. TrueFISP and T2-FLAIR images were acquired before treatment and every fifth fraction. TrueFISP-based extended resection cavity (cavity/tumor residue) and FLAIR-hyperintense volumes were contoured and analyzed longitudinally. Volume changes were stratified among early (SIM-f5) and late (f5-last fraction) phase and changes >±10% were deemed major. The exceedance of the volumes over the CTV and 95% isodose line was evaluated. Extended-resection-cavity- and FLAIR-contours derived from MR-linac imaging showed correspondence with those from diagnostic MRI (Pearson r > 0.96). In the extended resection cavity, 59%/27%/14% of analyzed patients showed major increase/major decrease/minor changes respectively. In FLAIR contours, the prevalences were 79%/0%/21% respectively. Differences between early and late volume changes were not statistically significant. The FLAIR contours exceeded CTV >1cc in 74% of patients, while the extended resection cavity exceeded the CTV and 95% isodose line >1cc in 27% and 18% respectively. No clinical or molecular parameter significantly predicted volumetric trajectories. Non-contrast MR-linac imaging reliably captures glioblastoma target volume dynamics during treatment. Volumetric changes are heterogeneous across patients and major changes can occur both early and late, underscoring the potential for serial imaging. Our data provide a rationale for further investigation of the clinical significance of these changes and their potential utility for individualized adaptive radiotherapy strategies.

title: Uncertainty-aware auto-segmentation enables adaptive radiotherapy planning of liver metastases.
abstract: Purpose Despite remarkable auto-segmentation performance and growing clinical adoption, models frequently fail to generalize beyond the training distribution. Therefore, this study aimed to develop and validate an uncertainty-aware segmentation pipeline that yields high delineation accuracy for liver cancer patients and reliably identifies safety-critical segmentation imperfections in radiotherapy. Materials and methods Datasets of n = 173 patients with 224 liver metastases were divided into training (n = 100), validation (n = 33), and test (n = 40). Each case included annotated T2-weighted magnetic resonance images. An nnU-Net segmented treatment-relevant organs and provided a margin-extended hepatic mask, which served as input to a second-stage SE-ResUNet for lesion delineation. Uncertainty was approximated via checkpoint ensembling under a cyclic learning-rate schedule, yielding entropy-based uncertainty maps and case-wise uncertainty scores. These guided an adaptive post-inference analysis consisting of (i) detection of potentially missed lesions and (ii) identification of problematic contours. Performance was evaluated on 40 patients (n = 52 lesions) using Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), 95%-Hausdorff-Distance (HD95), expected calibration error (ECE), uncertainty coverage, and the correlation between case-wise uncertainty scores and segmentation accuracy. Results Overall performance across treatment-relevant organs was DSC/HD95 = 0.89/4.8 mm; lesionsegmentation achieved DSC/HD95 = 0.86/4.9 mm. Uncertainty-guided post-processing, triggered in 14/40 cases, recovered 7 initially missed metastases, increasing lesion-level sensitivity from 84.6% (44/52) to 98.1% (51/52). Uncertainty estimates showed good calibration with ECE/uncertainty coverage for organs/lesion of 7.2/93.7% and 7.5/98.3%, and significant correlation between uncertainty/DSC (r = -0.802). Conclusion The proposed pipeline seamlessly integrates accurate organ/lesion segmentation, interpretable uncertainty, and anatomy-guided post-processing to detect safety-critical segmentation failures and enable trustworthy AI auto-segmentation in clinical routine.

title: Repeated metastasis-directed radiotherapy in patients with oligorecurrent prostate cancer: outcomes and risk stratification from a large multinational PSMA PET-guided cohort.
abstract: Background and purpose Repeated metastasis-directed radiotherapy (MDRT) is increasingly used in patients with metachronous oligometastatic prostate cancer. However, the efficacy and optimal patient selection criteria remain insufficiently defined. Material and methods Within the multinational PORTAL consortium, we evaluated outcomes of repeated MDRT in patients with prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography (PSMA-PET)-detected oligorecurrent hormone-sensitive prostate cancer undergoing ≥ 2 MDRT cycles. The primary endpoint was androgen deprivation therapy-free survival (ADT-FS), secondary endpoints included polymetastatic-free survival, next-line systemic therapy-free survival, and overall survival, all calculated from start of second MDRT. A multivariable Cox regression model was developed to predict ADT-FS, and its performance was evaluated by bootstrapped internal validation using discrimination (C-index) and calibration. Results A total of 177 patients were included. Median follow-up after second MDRT was 26.1 months. During follow-up, 86 patients initiated ADT, 59 developed polymetastatic disease, 38 received next-line systemic therapy, and 17 deaths occurred. Two-year ADT-FS was 50.2 % (95 % CI 41.4-58.3). Two-year polymetastatic-free, next-line systemic therapy-free, and overall survival were 64.4 % (95 % CI 55.4-72.0), 83.5 % (95 % CI 76.0-88.9), and 94.2 % (95 % CI 88.2-97.2), respectively. In the multivariable Cox regression model, a longer interval between first and second MDRT (HR 0.96 per month, 95 % CI 0.94-0.99; p = 0.003) and treatment of a single versus ≥ 2 new lesions (HR for ≥ 2 lesions 1.88, 95 % CI 1.22-2.90; p = 0.006) were independently associated with ADT-FS. Model discrimination was moderate (optimism-corrected C-index 0.68) with good calibration. Conclusions In this multicentre cohort of patients with PSMA PET-detected metachronous oligorecurrent prostate cancer undergoing repeated MDRT, favourable ADT-FS outcomes were observed, with approximately half of patients remaining ADT-free two years after second MDRT. Given the absence of a comparator group, these outcomes may reflect both the effects of treatment and favourable disease biology of patients who remained eligible for repeated MDRT. The interval between MDRT cycles, and the number of metastases, independently predicted ADT-FS and may support patient selection.

title: Photon FLASH spares radiation-induced lung injury and pulmonary hypertension in a preclinical model.
abstract: Introduction Ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) radiotherapy has shown significant promise in reducing normal tissue toxicities with equivalent tumour control compared to conventional (CONV) dose rates termed the FLASH effect. In this study, we compared radiation-induced lung injury and changes in the pulmonary circulation following localised right lung irradiation at UHDR and CONV exposures using photons. Methods Acute and late pulmonary radiation responses were assessed in pneumonitis (C3H/NeJ) and fibrosis prone (C57BL/6) mice. 18 Gy was delivered to the right lung at CONV (0.05 Gy/s), FLASH (76.2 Gy/s) and FLASH split dose (FSD, average 2.6 Gy/s) exposures. Early responses (72 h and 4 weeks after irradiation) were investigated by immunohistochemistry (Ly6G, F4/80), fluorescence staining (EdU) and serum profiling (cytokines and lipid peroxidation assays). Fibrosis was assessed at 30 weeks after irradiation by cone-beam CT (CBCT) analysis and quantification of collagen, senescence (p21) and TGF-β levels. Changes in pulmonary vasculature and transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) was assessed in C57BL/6 mice at 30 weeks to characterise changes in the pulmonary circulation associated with pulmonary hypertension (PH). Results At early timepoints, UHDR exposures led to reduced immune cell infiltration (neutrophils and macrophages) and tissue damage in comparison to CONV and FSD groups. Serum analysis supported FLASH sparing with decreased levels of markers associated with chronic inflammation and increased markers of tissue repair in comparison to CONV and FSD groups. At 30 weeks after irradiation at a UHDR, the lung parenchyma was structurally similar to controls (p = 0.33) with minimal collagen deposition supported by CBCT tissue density analysis. In contrast, CONV and FSD animals showed significant collagen deposition (p < 0.01) with thickened alveolar septa and reduced alveolar air spaces. UHDR exposures significantly reduced functional and histological metrics of PH (p < 0.05) compared to CONV. Conclusions UHDR photons significantly reduce radiation-induced pneumonitis and fibrosis with secondary effects on the pulmonary circulation sparing PH.

title: Deep learning-based spot weight generation for online adaptive IMPT: implementation and technical feasibility on a clinical delivery system.
abstract: Purpose To investigate the feasibility of a deep learning-based method for generating intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) spot weights to enable a faster, more automated workflow. Methods A 3D Attention U-Net with a masked mean absolute error loss generated spot weights from four input channels (optimized plan dose, reference dose, CT image, spot mask), using planned spot weights as labels, and trained and tested on prostate, brain, and lung cases. Robustness was evaluated on target dose metrics only. The workflow was validated in the Eclipse® treatment planning system and delivered on a ProBeam 360° system. Results For weights in the range 0-5, mean absolute errors were below 0.8 for the prostate and brain models (15.9% and 48.1% of all weights, respectively) and below 1.7 for the lung model (31.2%). Mean relative errors were below 10% for the prostate model (5-65, 83.7%), 20% for the brain model (5-65, 51.7%), and 40% for the lung model (5-110, 68.6%); the remaining weights lay above these ranges and accounted for <0.5% of all weights. Gamma passing rates within the body contours (2%, 2 mm, 10% dose threshold) were 99.73 ± 0.32%, 98.95 ± 0.86%, and 92.75 ± 3.52% for the prostate, brain, and lung models, respectively. All delivered plans met the clinical QA acceptance criteria. Conclusion The proposed framework demonstrates the technical feasibility of generating IMPT spot weights with deep learning and implementing them on a clinical delivery system. Further improvement is needed for heterogeneous sites such as the lung.

title: Uncertainty quantification for detecting out-of-distribution cases in deep learning segmentation of head and neck organs of interest.
abstract: Purpose Quality assurance (QA) of auto-segmentations is necessary for safe clinical deployment. Deep learning models are optimised for data similar to their training set, but reliability drops with out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. This study evaluates whether uncertainty quantification (UQ) can detect OOD inputs arising from distribution shift in head and neck organ of interest (OOI) auto-segmentation. Materials and methods Monte Carlo dropout-based uncertainty scores and geometric accuracy of nnU-Net models were evaluated in two experiments. First, as a proof-of-concept, we assessed whether uncertainty scores detect metal artefact (N = 10) from non-artefact cases (N = 10) on a baseline model (mixed training data, N = 620) and a no-metal model (artefact-free training data, N = 620). Second, in a clinically realistic experiment, we split a fine-tuning dataset by uncertainty score to obtain a narrow model (low-uncertainty cases, N = 21) and a broad model (high-uncertainty cases, N = 21). A held-out test set (N = 76) evaluated whether segmentation accuracy differed between uncertainty categories. Results Both experiments showed that uncertainty scores reflect the learned training distribution. In the supervised experiment, the no-metal model demonstrated greater uncertainty score separation between artefact and non-artefact cases (1.1 × 10 5 vs 0.6 × 10 5 ) than the baseline model (1.1 × 10 5 vs 0.8 × 10 5 ). In the unsupervised experiment, the narrow model performed significantly better on certain than uncertain cases (p = 0.04), while no difference was seen for the broad model (p = 0.34), which did include these cases in training. Conclusions Uncertainty quantification can detect distribution shifts in radiotherapy auto-segmentation. This could support automated QA workflows by identifying in-distribution cases and enabling the application of specialised models.

title: DAG-informed analysis of muscle characteristics and overall survival in patients receiving radical treatment for bladder cancer.
abstract: Background Reduced skeletal muscle (SM) quantity and quality may influence outcomes in bladder cancer, but most studies are associative and vulnerable to confounding and inconsistent covariate adjustment. We applied a directed acyclic graph (DAG)-informed framework to evaluate associations between computed tomography-derived SM characteristics and overall survival (OS) in patients receiving curative-intent radiotherapy-based bladder preservation or radical cystectomy. Methods This retrospective two-centre cohort study included patients treated between 2014 and 2024. Computed tomography imaging closest to definitive local therapy was analysed using an automated segmentation pipeline to quantify SM quantity, expressed as skeletal muscle index (SMI), and quality, expressed as intramuscular adipose tissue ratio (IMATR). A DAG was used to prespecify the adjustment strategy, and Cox models were fitted separately within radiotherapy and surgical cohorts. Results The final cohorts comprised 353 radiotherapy-treated and 117 surgically treated patients. In the radiotherapy cohort, higher SMI was associated with improved OS (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.66-0.94, p = 0.007), while higher IMATR was associated with worse OS (HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.04-1.48, p = 0.014). In the smaller surgical cohort, point estimates were directionally discordant with the radiotherapy findings and imprecise: SMI HR 1.35 (95% CI 0.99-1.85, p = 0.057) and IMATR HR 0.86 (95% CI 0.62-1.21, p = 0.39). Conclusions In this DAG-informed analysis, higher SMI and lower IMATR were associated with improved OS in radiotherapy-treated patients. Surgical estimates were imprecise and should be considered exploratory. These findings are hypothesis-generating and support further evaluation of CT-derived muscle characteristics as prognostic markers within radiotherapy-treated populations but cannot yet establish a differential benefit for radiotherapy vs cystectomy.

title: From contouring variability to dosimetric impact: a comprehensive assessment of online adaptive MR-guided SBRT for pancreatic cancer.
abstract: Purpose To quantify inter-physician contouring variability and evaluate its dosimetric impact in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) patients treated with daily online adaptive MR-guided stereotactic body radiotherapy (MRgSBRT), to assess safety and clinical robustness of online contouring. Methods Fifty treatment sessions from ten PDAC patients treated with 50 Gy in five fractions on a 1.5 T MR-Linac were retrospectively analyzed. During each treatment session ("online"), targets and organs-at-risk (OARs) within 3 cm of the tumor were delineated by seven physicians working on the MR-Linac. All structures were re-contoured offline by a single pancreatic-expert radiation oncologist ("reference"). Geometric agreement was assessed using Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), Mean Distance to Agreement (MDA), and 95 % Hausdorff Distance (HD95). Dosimetric analyses were performed on delivered treatment plans using both online and reference contours, with evaluation based on fraction-wise worst-case dose metrics. Results High geometric concordance was observed for stomach and duodenum, whereas smaller or anatomically complex structures (GTV, major vessels, bile duct) showed greater variability. Online GTVs were larger than reference contours. Despite these differences, target coverage (V50Gy and V35Gy) was maintained with online contours. While occasional per-fraction gastrointestinal (GI) dose constraint exceedances were identified using reference contours, fraction-wise worst-case analysis showed GI doses remained within clinical tolerance for nearly all patients. Conclusion Daily online adaptive MRgSBRT for PDAC provides robust target coverage and clinically acceptable OAR sparing, despite contouring variability. Multi-physician online contouring appears safe in clinical practice, although further improvements may be achieved through standardized contouring guidelines and harmonization strategies.

title: Ultrasound of the salivary glands in Sjögren's syndrome: a narrative review of its diagnostic and prognostic utility and clinical role.
abstract: Sjögren's Disease (SjD) is a systemic autoimmune disease whose classification criteria include a minor salivary gland biopsy (MSGB), an invasive procedure. Salivary gland ultrasound (SGUS) has emerged as a non-invasive, accessible and reliable tool for the evaluation of SjD. This narrative review analyses the evolution of SGUS, from the first scoring systems to the current consensus of the OMERACT group, which has enabled standardisation of the evaluation. The evidence on the diagnostic accuracy of SGUS, its correlation with MSGB and autoantibodies, and its ability to predict patient classification according to the 2016 ACR/EULAR criteria are analysed. In selected patients, SGUS may reduce the need for minor salivary gland biopsy, particularly in those positive for anti-Ro/SSA antibodies. In addition, it explores its potential role in prognostic stratification, lymphoma prediction, and treatment response monitoring, proposing an algorithm for its integration into daily clinical practice.

title: PET for Evaluation of Neurologic Diseases: Part one: Neurodegenerative Diseases.
abstract: This review of PET for evaluation of neurological diseases is divided into two parts; part one examines the clinical use of positron emission tomography (PET) in neurodegenerative diseases. FDG-PET can identify characteristic patterns of cerebral metabolism and help distinguish among neurodegenerative disorders. Amyloid and tau PET have expanding diagnostic and theranostic roles in Alzheimer's disease, including assessment of disease-specific pathology and treatment eligibility. FDOPA-PET evaluates presynaptic dopamine synthesis and supports assessment of Parkinson's disease and other parkinsonian syndromes. Combined with structural imaging and clinical evaluation, PET can improve diagnostic confidence, refine prognosis, and inform treatment decisions.

title: PET in Theranostics: Patient Selection, Treatment Planning, and Response Assessment.
abstract: Theranostics pairs molecular imaging with a therapeutic radiopharmaceutical directed at the same target, with PET assessing target expression, disease extent, interlesional heterogeneity, and FDG discordance. Three established applications are reviewed: PSMA PET-guided selection for lutetium-177-PSMA-617 in metastatic androgen pathway modulation-resistant prostate cancer, somatostatin receptor PET-guided peptide receptor radionuclide therapy in neuroendocrine tumors, and iodine-124/FDG PET within radioiodine therapy for differentiated thyroid cancer. Practical guidance covers patient selection, image interpretation, treatment planning, response assessment, and reporting. A key paradigm: diagnostic uptake confirms target availability but neither measures delivered dose nor guarantees response; biomarkers, dosimetry, and response frameworks remain variably validated.
